Structure the quality part on CTD Module 3, with a drug substance part and an investigational medicinal product part, and include the most up-to-date information relevant to the trial at the time of submission.

A simplified IMPD (CTR Annex I Table 1) may be used for an IMP authorised in the EU or an ICH country. If it is used unmodified, inside or outside the SmPC conditions, the SmPC can stand in for quality data. If it is modified (e.g. for blinding), submit P and A data (facilities and equipment, adventitious agents safety evaluation, novel excipients, solvents for reconstitution and diluents), with the SmPC covering the rest.
For a placebo IMP, the IMPD information requirements may be limited to quality data (CTR Annex I).
No GMP compliance documentation is needed for an IMP that is authorised and not modified, wherever it is manufactured (CTR Annex I, point 32).

If the IMP is not authorised in the EU, has no marketing authorisation from an ICH third country and is made outside the EU, submit a copy of the importer's Article 61 manufacturing/import authorisation (MIA) and an EU QP certification that manufacture meets GMP at least equivalent to EU GMP, unless MRA arrangements apply. In all other cases, submit a copy of the Article 61 authorisation.

Use the EudraLex Volume 10 QP declaration template for IMPs made in third countries. Give the EU CT number, IMP name(s), the MIA number, and the name, address and activities of each third-country site (Part A). Give the basis of the declaration (Part B): preferably an audit, recording who audited and when; without an audit, justify how equivalence to EU GMP is known.

Manufacturing or importing IMPs in the Union requires an authorisation under CTR Article 61. The holder must have, permanently and continuously, at least one QP who meets Article 49(2) and (3) of Directive 2001/83/EC.

The QP must ensure that each IMP batch manufactured in or imported into the Union complies with CTR Article 63 (GMP), and must certify it (Article 62). The sponsor must make the certification available at the request of the Member State concerned.

CTR Article 61(5) lists processes that do not need the Article 61 manufacturing/import authorisation. One is the preparation of radiopharmaceuticals used as diagnostic IMPs, carried out in hospitals, health centres or clinics by pharmacists or other persons legally authorised in the Member State. The list also covers certain hospital relabelling/repackaging and magistral/officinal preparations used as IMPs. Confirm eligibility, and any national requirements for these processes, against the article text.

Manufacture IMPs under the GMP principles of Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1569. These aim at consistency between batches of the same IMP used in the same or different trials, and require that changes during development be adequately documented and justified.

Apply the Detailed Commission guidelines on GMP for IMPs (C(2017) 8179, 8 December 2017), applicable since the CTR took effect. Keep a product specification file per IMP. QP certification must confirm the batch complies with that file and with the authorised CTA (IMPD).
IMP release is two-step: QP certification, then the sponsor's regulatory release (checking that the trial is authorised and conditions are met) before IMP ships to trial sites.

Do not cite the 2010 EudraLex Vol. 4 Annex 13 for EU/EEA trials. It covered trials under Directive 2001/20/EC. Since the CTR transition ended (30 January 2025), IMP GMP has been governed by Delegated Regulation 2017/1569 and the 2017 detailed Commission guideline on GMP for IMPs. IMP labelling follows CTR Annex VI.

Since 31 January 2023, all new initial EU/EEA CTAs must be submitted under the CTR through CTIS. Since 31 January 2025 only the CTR applies; trials ongoing beyond 30 January 2025 had to be transitioned to CTIS.

Submit a quality change as a Part I substantial modification in CTIS before implementing it if it is likely to have a substantial impact on subject safety or rights, or on data reliability and robustness. Changes the EMA IMP quality guideline treats as such include changes to the impurity profile, microbial contamination, viral safety or TSE risk, or stability where degradation products of concern may form.

Use EMA/CHMP/QWP/545525/2017 Rev. 2 (effective 31 January 2022) for IMPD quality data on chemically defined drug substances, synthetic peptides, herbal substances/preparations and chemically defined radioactive/radiolabelled substances, including radiopharmaceuticals.

Justify drug substance and IMP impurity acceptance criteria by the levels found in batches used in non-clinical (toxicology) and clinical studies, and review them as batch experience grows across development. Inadequately justified or incomplete specifications are among the most frequent IMPD deficiencies.

For phase 1, confirm that analytical methods are suitable and tabulate the validation parameters and acceptance limits; full validation reports are not required. For phase 2-3, provide a tabulated summary of the validation results.

Support the proposed IMP shelf life with stability data and include a stability protocol. Extending shelf life under the protocol in the authorised IMPD, with the stated commitments, need not be a substantial modification. Missing or insufficient stability data is a frequent IMPD deficiency.
Discuss and control potentially mutagenic impurities in the IMPD, taking into account the trial's dose and duration.

For biological/biotechnology-derived IMPs without a simplified IMPD, prepare the IMPD-Q under EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2 (effective 31 January 2022), covering biological, chemical and pharmaceutical quality.
Address adventitious agent and viral safety (raw material control, cell bank testing and viral clearance capacity of the purification process) from the first clinical trial onward.

Support manufacturing process changes during clinical development with a risk-based comparability exercise between pre- and post-change material, especially after batches used in non-clinical or earlier clinical studies.
Include a biological activity/potency assay in release specifications for biological IMPs. Its validation status may be phase-appropriate, maturing towards confirmatory trials.

Prepare investigational ATMP CTAs (gene therapy, somatic cell therapy, tissue-engineered and combined ATMPs) under EMA/CAT/22473/2025, in effect since 1 July 2025. It applies a risk-based approach under which the extent of quality, non-clinical and clinical data may be adapted to identified risks.

Manufacture investigational and authorised ATMPs under EudraLex Volume 4 Part IV (risk-based GMP specific to ATMPs), not the general IMP GMP guideline. Part IV is under revision (EMA concept paper EMA/INS/GMP/48771/2025), so confirm the version in force before citing it.

An EU MAA must include Module 3 (3.2.S drug substance, 3.2.P drug product, 3.2.A appendices, 3.2.R regional information) and a Module 2.3 Quality Overall Summary in CTD format, under Article 8(3) and Annex I of Directive 2001/83/EC. The quality module is similar whatever the legal basis of the MA and is kept up to date after authorisation through variations.

A valid EDQM CEP for the active substance may replace the corresponding 3.2.S data. Include a copy of the CEP and provide any data it does not cover, such as tests or properties outside the monograph.

Under the ASMF procedure, the active substance manufacturer sends the Restricted (confidential) Part directly to the authorities and the Applicant's Part to the applicant. The applicant includes the Applicant's Part and a letter of access in the MAA.
With an MAA, and with variations adding active substance manufacturers, submit a QP declaration (EMA template), based on audit, that active substance manufacture complies with EU GMP.

For standard manufacturing processes, an EU MAA may include a process validation scheme in 3.2.R in place of full-scale validation data, provided validation is completed before commercial release. Non-standard processes need validation data at submission.

For an integral drug-device combination, include evidence that the device part conforms to the relevant MDR Annex I general safety and performance requirements: an EU declaration of conformity, a notified body certificate or a notified body opinion (MDR Article 117, applicable since 26 May 2021).
For materials of animal or human origin, place TSE risk information (e.g. TSE certificates of suitability or equivalent data) in EU 3.2.R, and adventitious agent safety data in 3.2.A.2.

Evaluate the nitrosamine risk for the active substance and finished product. Where a risk is identified, perform confirmatory testing with sufficiently sensitive validated methods and control nitrosamines at or below the acceptable intake. MAHs implement any needed changes through variations.

For NDSRIs without compound-specific data, set acceptable intake limits with the CPCA, introduced in revision 16 of EMA's nitrosamine Q&A: 18 ng/day for category 1, 100 ng/day for category 2, 400 ng/day for category 3 and 1500 ng/day for categories 4-5. First check the Q&A's current list of established limits.

Classify post-approval CMC changes under Regulation (EC) No 1234/2008 and the Commission variations guidelines: Type IA/IAIN (do-and-tell), Type IB (notify and wait), Type II (prior approval; a change that may significantly affect quality, safety or efficacy) or extension. Submit the updated Module 3 sections with the variation. Classification of the same change can differ between EEA authorities, so justify the proposed category.

Classify each change against the variations framework in force on its submission date: Regulation (EC) No 1234/2008 as amended by Delegated Regulation (EU) 2024/1701, and the revised Commission variations classification guidelines that replace the 2013 guidelines (2013/C 223/01). Check the application dates of both in the Official Journal before relying on a classification code.
A QP of an EU/EEA MIA holder must certify each commercial batch, including imported batches, before release, per EudraLex Volume 4 Annex 16.

As of 2026-10, cite Directive 2001/83/EC Annex I and Regulation (EC) No 726/2004 as the operative dossier requirements. The pharmaceutical reform (COM(2023) 192/193; procedures 2023/0132 and 2023/0131(COD)) was not confirmed as adopted or applicable, so treat its provisions (e.g. the platform technology approach) as pending.

requirements.phase: commercial manufacture; check applicability to sterile IMPs
requirements.statement: Manufacture sterile medicinal products under a documented, lifecycle contamination control strategy, as the 2022 revision of EU GMP Annex 1 requires. Integrity-test sterilised filter assemblies before use (PUPSIT, section 8.87); where PUPSIT is not feasible, document a risk-based justification.

Where an auxiliary medicinal product used in an EU/EEA trial (e.g. a challenge agent or rescue medication) is not authorised, or is an authorised product that has been modified, it must be manufactured under GMP or at least an equivalent standard.

An IND must contain a CMC section describing the composition, manufacture and control of the drug substance and the drug product. In every phase it must be enough to assure proper identification, quality, purity and strength, with the amount scaled to the phase, proposed study duration, dosage form and information otherwise available.

In an initial Phase 1 IND, focus the CMC section on identifying and controlling raw materials and the new drug substance. FDA does not expect final drug substance and drug product specifications until the end of the investigational process.

For the drug substance, the IND must give: a description including its physical, chemical or biological characteristics; the manufacturer's name and address; the general method of preparation; acceptable limits and analytical methods for identity, strength, quality and purity; and enough information to support stability during the toxicology studies and the planned clinical studies.

For the drug product, the IND must give: all components used in manufacture, including any that do not appear in the final product, with quantitative composition where applicable; the manufacturer's name and address; a brief general description of manufacturing and packaging; acceptable limits and analytical methods for identity, strength, quality and purity; and enough information to assure stability during the planned clinical studies.
For any placebo used in a controlled clinical trial, include a brief general description of its composition, manufacture and control.

Submit a copy of all labels and labeling to be provided to each investigator. The immediate package must carry the statement 'Caution: New Drug - Limited by Federal (or United States) law to investigational use.' Labeling must not be false or misleading or claim the drug is safe or effective for the use under investigation.

Include either a claim for categorical exclusion under 21 CFR 25.30 or 25.31 or an environmental assessment under 21 CFR 25.40. Action on an IND is categorically excluded under 25.31(e) unless extraordinary circumstances apply.
A reference to the current edition of the USP-NF may satisfy the relevant IND CMC requirements for compendial articles.

requirements.phase: all phases (IND), especially at scale-up and between phases
requirements.statement: As development moves from pilot-scale to larger-scale production, supplement the original CMC information through information amendments. Each must be prominently labelled 'Information Amendment: Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Control' and contain a statement of its nature and purpose plus an organized data submission. Where feasible, submit no more often than every 30 days.
File the IND annual report within 60 days of the anniversary of the IND's effective date. It must summarize any significant manufacturing or microbiological changes made during the past year.

Open the CMC section by stating whether the chemistry or manufacturing of the drug substance or drug product presents any signals of potential human risk. If it does, discuss the signals and the steps proposed to monitor for those risks, or explain why they can be dismissed.

Relate the clinical drug product to the material used in the animal toxicology studies that support safety. Describe any chemistry or manufacturing differences between them and how those differences might affect the safety profile.

For Phase 1, preliminary tabular stability data on representative material may be submitted. Neither detailed stability data nor the stability protocol should be submitted, and validation data and established specifications need not be submitted at this initial stage.

For an original FIH Phase 1 IND (CDER small molecule), FDA generally expects at least 1 month of stability data from a representative drug substance lot, and from a representative drug product lot, when no degradation is observed. Stability data on the specific clinical lot are not required, and initial data need not cover the full duration of the proposed studies. Information supporting drug product stability during the planned studies is still expected at submission.

For original FIH Phase 1 INDs of CDER-regulated small molecules and recombinant biologics, analytical method validation data are not expected. Process controls not directly related to product safety need not be specified.

For original FIH Phase 1 INDs of CDER recombinant biologics, FDA's 2026 clarification makes these points: (a) full characterization with multiple orthogonal methods is not expected; (b) a product-specific viral clearance study is listed as generally not needed at FIH (check the PDF for the accompanying risk-assessment wording); (c) a potency assay is not expected for simple proteins shown to have no higher-order structure; and (d) potency characterization results may be enough to start the trial if quality-control method development is not complete.

For Phase 2 and 3 INDs, submit CMC safety information through information amendments before the relevant phase starts; it may be filed during Phase 1. Corroborating CMC information not critical to safety can be generated during Phase 2 or 3 and summarized in annual reports. This 2003 guidance does not apply to botanicals, protein drugs from natural sources or biotechnology, or other biologics.

Most Phase 1 investigational drugs, including biological drugs, are exempt from 21 CFR Part 211 under 21 CFR 210.2(c). They remain subject to statutory CGMP (FD&C Act 501(a)(2)(B)), applied as described in FDA's July 2008 Phase 1 CGMP guidance. That guidance does not apply to HCT/Ps regulated solely under PHS Act section 361.

Investigational drugs for Phase 2 and 3 trials must be manufactured under 21 CFR Part 211. Once a sponsor has made an investigational drug available for a Phase 2 or 3 trial, or the drug has been lawfully marketed, any later Phase 1 use of that drug must also comply with Part 211.

Exploratory IND studies (early Phase 1, very limited exposure, no therapeutic or diagnostic intent, such as microdose studies) can rely on the regulations' flexibility to submit less CMC and preclinical data, as described in FDA's 2006 Exploratory IND guidance.

eCTD is mandatory for NDAs, ANDAs and BLAs since 2017-05-05, and for commercial INDs and all master file submissions since 2018-05-05. Later amendments, supplements and reports must also be in eCTD even if the original was not. Noncommercial INDs (investigator-sponsored, research and expanded-access INDs) are exempt. Short-term waivers follow the criteria in section III.E of the guidance.

Since 2024-09-16, CDER and CBER accept new applications in eCTD v4.0; v3.2.2 remains supported. Only new applications may start in v4.0 because forward compatibility is not yet available. FDA will give advance notice before accepting v4.0 only.

Organize gene therapy IND CMC information under CTD Module 3, including 3.2.A.1 Facilities and Equipment and 3.2.A.2 Adventitious Agents Safety Evaluation. Not every CTD section must be completed in the original IND. A Module 2.3 QOS summarizing the manufacturing process, controls and qualification of components and starting materials is recommended. Process validation is not required for early-stage manufacturing.

Put risk assessments for human- or animal-derived materials in 3.2.A.2, covering viral clearance, inactivation steps or adventitious agent testing of source material, together with representative certificates of analysis. For replication-incompetent vectors, show the absence of replication-competent virus.

Under CBER's 2011 potency guidance, potency information supports cell and gene therapy INDs at every phase. Suitable potency assay(s) should be in place before studies meant to provide primary evidence of effectiveness. Lot-release potency assays must be validated to support a BLA. The December 2023 draft 'Potency Assurance' guidance, intended to replace the 2011 guidance, frames potency as a multifaceted control strategy.

Under CBER's May 2026 CMC flexibilities guidance, cell and gene therapy sponsors may: use relatively permissive release acceptance criteria early if safety is not compromised, but define acceptance criteria before Phase 2/3; support minor, low-risk manufacturing changes with limited comparability data, submitted before post-change product is given; and justify the number of PPQ batches scientifically instead of defaulting to three. FDA may also allow flexible commercial specifications when lots are few.

Run a risk assessment for every cell and gene therapy manufacturing change and scale any comparability study to that risk. FDA's July 2023 draft on Manufacturing Changes and Comparability (not for implementation) and the May 2026 flexibilities guidance describe this approach.

For early trials with live biotherapeutic products, follow CBER's LBP CMC guidance. Its June 2016 update explains when the label of a commercially available product may satisfy the IND CMC requirements.

An IND, NDA, ANDA, amendment or supplement may incorporate a DMF by reference only with the holder's written authorization (letter of authorization). Per FDA DMF guidance, the LOA should give: date; holder name; DMF number; the person(s) authorized; the specific product(s); the section or page numbers referenced; a commitment that the DMF is current and will be complied with; and the authorizing official's signature, typed name and title.

The DMF must contain a complete list of everyone currently authorized to reference it, identifying the information each may incorporate. If authorization is limited to particular products, the list must name each product and its application number if known. Since 2018-05-05 all DMF submissions, including LOAs, amendments and annual reports, must be in eCTD with no waivers.

A BLA may not incorporate drug substance, drug substance intermediate or drug product information by reference to a master file; it must be in the BLA itself. The exception is transition (deemed-BLA) products that referenced such information at approval. INDs for products to be licensed under the PHS Act may incorporate any master file information. Effective 2024-03-13.

Assess the risk of nitrosamine impurities, including NDSRIs, in the API and drug product as early in development as possible. Complete the risk assessment and any confirmatory testing before the original NDA where feasible; otherwise submit them by amendment as soon as possible after filing. Inform FDA and amend the application if levels exceed the acceptable intake limit.

Set NDSRI limits using FDA's predicted carcinogenic potency categorization and the AI limits on FDA's live 'CDER Nitrosamine Impurity Acceptable Intake Limits' webpage. For approved or marketed products, NDSRI confirmatory testing was due by 2025-08-01. Under the June 2025 update, a progress report may be submitted where mitigation was not complete, covering methods, results, root cause, mitigation and timeline.

Control elemental impurities in US drug products with a risk-based approach consistent with ICH Q3D(R2). R2 adds cutaneous and transcutaneous PDEs. Q3D does not apply to drug products used during clinical research, but its principles are useful as the commercial process is developed.

Assess and control DNA-reactive (mutagenic) impurities under ICH M7(R2) during clinical development and in marketing applications. Less-than-lifetime acceptable intakes apply to clinical treatment durations of up to 1 month, 1-12 months, and over 1 year through the end of Phase 3. Compound-specific AIs follow the M7(R2) Addendum.

Apply the ICH Q3A(R2) and Q3B(R2) reporting, identification and qualification thresholds to impurities in new chemically synthesized drug substances and to degradation products in the drug products made from them. Justify the limits in the specification justification sections.
Control residual solvents to ICH Q3C PDEs. Q3C(R8), adopted by FDA in December 2021, adds PDEs for 2-methyltetrahydrofuran, cyclopentyl methyl ether and tert-butyl alcohol.

Choose specification tests and justify acceptance criteria per ICH Q6A (chemical substances) or ICH Q6B (biotechnological and biological products). Present them in 3.2.S.4.1/3.2.P.5.1 with justification in 3.2.S.4.5/3.2.P.5.6.

Validate analytical procedures under ICH Q2(R2) and develop them under ICH Q14 (both FDA final guidances since March 2024). Q2(R2) covers procedures that use spectroscopic data. Q14's enhanced approach can support risk-based post-approval changes to analytical procedures.

NDAs, ANDAs, BLAs and supplements must include analytical procedures and methods validation data documenting identity, strength, quality, purity and potency of the drug substance and drug product. On request, the applicant must send samples so FDA laboratories can test them and validate the applicant's procedures. Requested samples cover the drug product, the drug substance used to make it, and non-compendial reference standards and blanks, with descriptive information and results.

The NDA CMC section (21 CFR 314.50(d)(1)) must give a full drug substance description, including physical and chemical characteristics and stability, manufacturer, method of synthesis or isolation and purification, process controls, and specifications. Specifications must include tests, analytical procedures and acceptance criteria for stability, sterility, particle size and crystalline form where relevant. For the drug product it must give all components (including those not in the final product), the composition, specifications for each component, each manufacturer, and the manufacturing and packaging procedures.

A BLA must include: a full description of manufacturing methods; stability data through the proposed dating period; representative samples; summaries of lot test results; label, enclosure and container specimens; and the address of each manufacturing location. Establishments must meet the applicable GMP requirements in 21 CFR parts 210, 211, 600, 606 and 820.

US Module 3 regional section 3.2.R holds: executed batch records (drug substance in 3.2.R.1.S, which may reference a DMF, otherwise executed plus blank master records; drug product in 3.2.R.1.P.1 with equipment specified and packaging records); comparability protocols (3.2.R.2.S/3.2.R.2.P); and the methods validation package (3.2.R.3.S for non-USP drug substances, 3.2.R.3.P).

A comparability protocol sets the specific tests, studies and acceptance criteria that will show a planned CMC change has no adverse effect on identity, strength, quality, purity or potency. Submit it in the original NDA, ANDA or BLA, or later as a prior approval supplement. An approved protocol can allow a reduced reporting category for the change.

Validate commercial processes on a lifecycle basis: process design, process qualification including PPQ, and continued process verification. PPQ monitoring must give statistical confidence within and between batches, and data from commercial-scale batches should support the decision to begin commercial distribution. FDA's 2011 guidance does not mandate a fixed three-batch approach.

Applications using continuous manufacturing should cover the development, implementation, operation and lifecycle-management elements described in ICH Q13 (FDA final, March 2023). Q13 replaced FDA's 2019 draft 'Quality Considerations for Continuous Manufacturing'.

For biotechnology products from human or animal cell lines, document viral safety with the risk-based principles and mitigation strategies of ICH Q5A(R2), including the data a marketing application needs. FDA adopted Q5A(R2) as final guidance in January 2024, replacing Q5A (1998).

When the manufacturing process of a biotechnological or biological product changes, show comparability of pre- and post-change product per ICH Q5E. The evidence must show no adverse impact on quality, safety or efficacy.

Design registration stability studies per ICH Q1A(R2). Test attributes susceptible to change during storage that are likely to influence quality, safety or efficacy (physical, chemical, biological, microbiological), using validated stability-indicating analytical procedures.

Keep applying Q1A(R2), Q1B, Q1C, Q1D, Q1E and Q5C for stability. The consolidated ICH Q1, which would replace them and add ATMPs, vaccines, complex biologics and combination products, is an FDA draft (June 2025). ICH Step 4 is projected for November 2026, and as of 2026-10-04 it is not a requirement.

Treat ICH Q3E (extractables and leachables; FDA draft December 2025, Step 4 projected June 2027) and FDA's August 2026 draft container closure guidance as current thinking, not requirements. The 1999 container closure guidance and its 2002 Q&A stay in effect until the new guidance is final.

Keep structuring Module 2.3 and Module 3 to M4Q (FDA M4Q guidance, August 2001). ICH M4Q(R2), which would restructure both, is only an FDA draft (January 2026) with no confirmed effective date as of 2026-10-04.

Under ICH Q12 (FDA final, May 2021), applicants may define established conditions and use post-approval change management protocols and a product lifecycle management document. These make post-approval CMC changes more predictable.

Present pharmaceutical development (3.2.P.2) per ICH Q8(R2). Present drug substance process description, controls and process development (3.2.S.2.2-3.2.S.2.6) per ICH Q11. Apply quality risk management per ICH Q9(R1).

If an AI model produces data or information used to support a regulatory decision on product quality, including in manufacturing, define its context of use, assess model risk, and plan and document a credibility assessment. FDA's January 2025 draft guidance sets out a seven-step framework for this and was still a draft as of 2026-10.
Submit an accurate and complete English translation of any part of the IND not in English, plus a copy of each original literature publication that is translated.

Sponsors of CDER- or CBER-regulated products for serious conditions with unmet need on accelerated clinical timelines can seek early CMC engagement through FDA's CMC Development and Readiness Pilot, which runs through FY2027 under PDUFA VII. This is described in FDA's July 2026 CMC readiness strategy document and is an option, not a requirement.

For registration, submit long-term stability data covering at least 12 months on at least three primary batches, plus 6 months of accelerated data. Continue long-term testing until it covers the proposed re-test period (drug substance) or shelf life (drug product).

General-case storage conditions: long-term 25°C ± 2°C / 60% RH ± 5% RH, or 30°C ± 2°C / 65% RH ± 5% RH. Intermediate 30°C ± 2°C / 65% RH ± 5% RH, triggered by significant change at accelerated when long-term is 25°C/60% RH. Accelerated 40°C ± 2°C / 75% RH ± 5% RH for 6 months. Refrigerated, frozen and semi-permeable-container cases have their own conditions in Q1A(R2).

If long-term data on primary batches do not yet cover the proposed re-test period or shelf life at approval, commit to continuing the studies after approval. Record the post-approval stability protocol and stability commitment in 3.2.S.7.2 and 3.2.P.8.2.

Photostability testing has two parts: forced degradation, which evaluates photosensitivity for method development and degradation pathways, and confirmatory testing. Confirmatory testing is normally done on one batch, with up to two more batches if results are equivocal. Minimum confirmatory exposure is 1.2 million lux hours of visible light and 200 watt hours/m² of near-UV energy.

The stability protocol for a new dosage form filed by the original applicant should follow Q1A(R2). In justified cases, a reduced stability database at submission (e.g., 6 months accelerated and 6 months long-term from ongoing studies) may be acceptable.

Bracketing (testing only the extremes of factors such as strength or container size/fill) and matrixing (testing a subset of samples at each time point) may be used in formal stability studies only with justification. Describe the design and its justification in the stability summary.

Where the Q1E decision tree permits extrapolation (e.g., room-temperature storage with no significant change at accelerated), the proposed re-test period or shelf life is capped. If the data are amenable to and supported by statistical analysis, it may be up to twice the long-term period, but no more than 12 months beyond it. Otherwise it may be up to 1.5 times, but no more than 6 months beyond. Other branches of the decision tree (e.g., significant change at accelerated, refrigerated storage) have different limits.

The consolidated ICH Q1 (Step 2b draft, 11 April 2025) will supersede Q1A(R2), Q1B, Q1C, Q1D, Q1E and Q5C once it reaches Step 4, which is targeted for November 2026. Until ICH confirms Step 4, Q1A(R2)-Q1E and Q5C remain the applicable ICH stability standards; cite Q1 text only as a draft.

Q1F (Climatic Zones III and IV) was withdrawn in June 2006, and ICH left storage conditions for those zones to the regions and WHO. Do not cite Q1F; apply the receiving authority's or WHO's climatic-zone requirements.

Validate analytical procedures used for release and stability testing of commercial drug substances and products against Q2(R2) to show they are fit for their intended purpose. Relevant performance characteristics include specificity/selectivity, range (including response and lower range limit), accuracy and precision. Q2(R2) can also be applied, risk-based, to other procedures in the control strategy. Validation data go in 3.2.S.4.3 and 3.2.P.5.3.

Q2(R2) is scoped to release and stability testing of commercial drug substances and products. It does not set phase-specific validation expectations for clinical-trial material; the extent of validation expected in an IND, CTA or IMPD is phase-appropriate and set by the receiving authority's clinical-trial guidance.

Analytical procedures may be developed under a minimal or an enhanced approach. The enhanced approach (analytical target profile, risk assessment, knowledge of parameter ranges, analytical procedure control strategy) can support proposed Established Conditions and lower reporting categories for post-approval procedure changes under Q12. Define the analytical procedure control strategy before validation and confirm it afterwards.

Drug substance impurity thresholds for a maximum daily dose of 2 g/day or less: reporting 0.05%; identification 0.10% or 1.0 mg/day total daily intake, whichever is lower; qualification 0.15% or 1.0 mg/day, whichever is lower. Above 2 g/day: reporting 0.03%, identification 0.05%, qualification 0.05%.

Where applicable, the drug substance specification lists each specified identified impurity, each specified unidentified impurity, any unspecified impurity (limit no higher than the identification threshold), total impurities, residual solvents and inorganic impurities. Impurities above the qualification threshold must be qualified or justified.

Q3A(R2) and Q3B(R2) are not intended to apply to drug substances or products used during clinical research stages. Their thresholds bind on registration specifications, and health authorities generally expect sponsors to work towards them as development progresses. Clinical-phase impurity expectations come from regional IND/CTA guidance.

Drug product specifications address degradation products of the drug substance and reaction products with excipients or the container closure. Report, identify and qualify them against Q3B(R2) thresholds, which depend on maximum daily dose, and justify acceptance criteria from batch and stability data.

Classify residual solvents under Q3C. Class 1 solvents should not be used unless their use is unavoidable for a product with a significant therapeutic advance, in which case levels are restricted to the Q3C Class 1 limits. Class 2 solvents are limited by PDE, using Option 1 (ppm) or Option 2 (summed daily exposure). Class 3 solvents at 50 mg/day or less (5000 ppm or 0.5% under Option 1) are acceptable without justification.

Q3C does not apply to potential new drug substances, excipients or drug products used during clinical research stages, nor to existing marketed products. Residual-solvent expectations for IND/CTA material come from regional guidance, which commonly references Q3C principles.

Q3C(R10), in development, is revising the PDEs for N,N-dimethylformamide, dichloromethane and ethylene glycol. Q3C(R9) limits apply until R10 is adopted; flag control strategies that rely on DMF, DCM or ethylene glycol limits for re-evaluation.

Perform and summarise a product risk assessment for elemental impurities from all potential sources (drug substance, excipients, water, manufacturing equipment, container closure) against route-specific PDEs: oral, parenteral, inhalation, and cutaneous/transcutaneous from R2. The assessment may use a component or a finished-product approach. If total levels are consistently below the control threshold of 30% of the PDE, no additional controls are required; otherwise set controls such as specification limits.
Q3D(R2) does not apply to drug products used during clinical research stages of development. Its principles can be useful while the commercial process is developed.

Draft Q3E (Step 2b) proposes a risk-based framework for extractables and leachables from manufacturing components, packaging and delivery devices. It uses a product-specific safety concern threshold (the lowest of the M7 TTC, a route- and duration-specific qualification threshold and any local-toxicity threshold) and three leachable classes: Class 1 to be avoided, needing compound-specific limits; Class 2 to be limited, assessed compound-specifically above the threshold; and Class 3 of low toxicity, with supporting monographs. Safety of elemental leachables stays under Q3D. Q3E is not final: cite it as a draft and rely on current regional E&L expectations until Step 4.

A pharmacopoeial general chapter evaluated in a Q4B topic-specific annex (e.g., dissolution, disintegration, uniformity of dosage units, sterility, bacterial endotoxins, microbiological examination of non-sterile products) may be treated as interchangeable across the ICH regions, subject to that annex's conditions and regional implementation. When relying on interchangeability, cite the annex and meet its conditions.

requirements.phase: all phases (Q5A(R2) defines the marketing-application data set; clinical-stage extent per regional guidance)
requirements.statement: Show viral safety of cell-line-derived biotechnology products through complementary approaches: selection and testing of cell lines and raw materials, viral clearance studies, and virus testing at appropriate production steps. Q5A(R2) accepts next-generation sequencing as an alternative to traditional in vivo, in vitro and PCR adventitious-virus tests, based on risk assessment. Present the evaluation in 3.2.A.2 with cross-references to 3.2.S.2.

Under Q5A(R2), prior knowledge (e.g., in-house platform data) may replace some product-specific viral clearance data if appropriately justified. Viral clearance studies on used (cycled) resin are not required for Protein A chromatography. Other chromatography steps still need used-resin evaluation, though justified prior knowledge may substitute for product-specific studies.

For r-DNA-derived proteins, describe and characterise the expression construct (origin of the coding sequence, vector construction, coding-region nucleotide sequence). Confirm the coding sequence and genetic stability in production cells, including cells cultured to the limit of in vitro cell age used for production.

Document the cell substrate's origin and history, how the production cell line was generated, and the Master and Working Cell Bank system. Characterise the banks for identity, purity (microbial and viral/adventitious agents, cross-contamination) and stability through the proposed in vitro cell age.

Base the shelf life of biotechnological/biological drug substances and products on real-time, real-temperature data from at least 3 batches representative of manufacturing scale. If a shelf life of more than 6 months is requested, submit at least 6 months of data; shorter periods are decided case by case.

After a manufacturing process change to a biotechnological/biological product, during development or after approval, run a comparability exercise. It should show that pre- and post-change product are highly similar and that any differences in quality attributes have no adverse impact on safety or efficacy. Add nonclinical or clinical bridging when analytical data are insufficient.

Specifications include the universal tests (description, identification, assay, impurities) plus specific tests as applicable. Drug substance examples: particle size, polymorphic form, chiral purity, water, microbial limits. Drug product examples: dissolution, uniformity of dosage units. Justify acceptance criteria with the Q6A decision trees and with development, batch and stability data.

Characterise biotech products (physicochemical properties, biological activity, immunochemical properties, purity, impurities, quantity) to support the specification. The specification covers identity, purity and impurities, potency and quantity. Justify acceptance criteria from preclinical/clinical lots, manufacturing-consistency lots, stability and development data.

Q6(R1), in development, will merge Q6A and Q6B and extend specification principles to modalities such as cell and gene therapies. Q6A and Q6B apply until Q6(R1) reaches Step 4. Reported targets are Step 2 in November 2026 and Step 4 in June 2027 (unverified).
Q7 API GMP applies from the introduction of the API starting material into the process. In a convergent synthesis, Q7 GMP applies to each branch from the first use of a starting material.

APIs for clinical trials fall under Q7 Section 19. Controls should be consistent with the development stage of the drug product, and process and test procedures should be flexible enough to change as process knowledge grows. Not all controls in Q7's earlier sections suit investigational APIs.

At minimum, 3.2.P.2 identifies the drug substance, excipient, container-closure and manufacturing-process aspects critical to product quality and justifies the control strategy. An enhanced (QbD) approach adds a QTPP, CQAs and a risk assessment linking material attributes and process parameters to CQAs, and may propose a design space. The design space is subject to regulatory assessment, and movement within an approved design space is not a change.

Base quality risk evaluation on scientific knowledge linked to patient protection, with effort, formality and documentation proportionate to the level of risk. Q9(R1) adds expectations on formality, managing subjectivity, risk-based decision-making and product-availability risks.

A Q10 pharmaceutical quality system applies four elements across the lifecycle: process performance and product quality monitoring; corrective and preventive action (CAPA); change management; and management review of process performance and product quality.

Q11 governs 3.2.S.2.2-3.2.S.2.6: process description (including all steps that affect the drug substance impurity profile), control of materials and justification of starting materials, controls of critical steps and intermediates, process validation/evaluation, and process development history. The control strategy links to the specification in 3.2.S.4.

Justify each proposed starting material. Include a flow diagram of the synthetic route(s) marking the starting materials, describe the formation, fate and purge of impurities, and show how the starting-material specification supports the control strategy. A commercially available chemical generally needs no justification; a custom-synthesised starting material must be justified against Q11 principles.

Under Q12, the applicant may identify Established Conditions, with rationale in the relevant CTD sections, and propose risk-based reporting categories for changes to them. It may also propose PACMPs. A PLCM document summarises the ECs, reporting categories, PACMPs and post-approval CMC commitments; it is filed with the original application, or with a variation/supplement for marketed products. Regional uptake of these tools varies.

For continuous manufacturing, describe the control strategy, process dynamics and residence time distribution (which support material traceability and diversion), process monitoring, and the batch definition. Batch size may be defined by quantity of output, quantity of input, or run time at a defined mass flow rate; it may be a range, or another justified approach may be used.

requirements.phase: marketing (CTD format also used for many IND/CTA quality sections)
requirements.statement: The CTD has five modules. Module 1 (regional administrative information) is region-specific; Modules 2-5 are common to all regions. The quality summary is Module 2.3, and the quality body of data is Module 3.

Module 3 drug substance sections are: 3.2.S.1 General Information; 3.2.S.2 Manufacture; 3.2.S.3 Characterisation; 3.2.S.4 Control of Drug Substance; 3.2.S.5 Reference Standards or Materials; 3.2.S.6 Container Closure System; 3.2.S.7 Stability.

Module 3 drug product sections are: 3.2.P.1 Description and Composition of the Drug Product; 3.2.P.2 Pharmaceutical Development; 3.2.P.3 Manufacture; 3.2.P.4 Control of Excipients; 3.2.P.5 Control of Drug Product; 3.2.P.6 Reference Standards or Materials; 3.2.P.7 Container Closure System; 3.2.P.8 Stability.

3.2.A Appendices covers A.1 Facilities and Equipment, A.2 Adventitious Agents Safety Evaluation and A.3 Novel Excipients. 3.2.R Regional Information holds region-specific drug substance and drug product information; M4Q directs applicants to regional guidance for its content, so items such as US executed batch records or the EU drug product process validation scheme are defined by regional guidance, not M4Q. 3.3 holds Literature References.
The Module 2.3 Quality Overall Summary follows the scope and outline of Module 3. It should not include information, data or justification not already included in Module 3 or elsewhere in the CTD.

Use the M4Q Q&A / location-issues guidance to decide where to place quality information that could fit in more than one CTD section, and cross-reference the linked sections for parameters such as polymorphism and particle size.

Draft M4Q(R2) (Step 2, May 2025) would make Module 2.3 the primary basis for assessment. Its components are 2.3.1 General Information, 2.3.2 Overall Development and Control Strategy, 2.3.3 Core Quality Information, development summaries/justifications, and optional 2.3.5 Product Lifecycle Management and 2.3.6 Product Quality Benefit-Risk; Module 3 becomes the repository of supporting data. Section numbering may change before Step 4, targeted for June 2027. M4Q(R1) remains the applicable format.

Assess actual and potential impurities and degradants for mutagenic potential. First search databases and literature for carcinogenicity and bacterial mutagenicity data. Where none exist, run (Q)SAR with two complementary methodologies (expert rule-based and statistical-based) plus expert review, or an Ames test. Place each impurity in one of the five M7 classes to decide its control.

The default lifetime TTC-based acceptable intake is 1.5 µg/day per mutagenic impurity, corresponding to a theoretical excess lifetime cancer risk below 1 in 100,000. Less-than-lifetime acceptable intakes are 120 µg/day for 1 month or less, 20 µg/day for more than 1 to 12 months, 10 µg/day for more than 1 to 10 years, and 1.5 µg/day for more than 10 years to lifetime. Compound-specific AIs/PDEs, such as those in the M7(R2) Addendum, take precedence where available. The TTC does not apply to cohort-of-concern compounds (aflatoxin-like, N-nitroso, alkyl-azoxy).

With one or two Class 2 or Class 3 mutagenic impurities, apply the individual limit to each. With three or more, also limit total mutagenic impurities to the M7 total-intake limits (understood as 120 µg/day for 1 month or less, 60 µg/day for more than 1 to 12 months, 30 µg/day for more than 1 to 10 years, and 5 µg/day for more than 10 years to lifetime; verify these values against M7 text before quoting). Each impurity must still meet its own TTC-based or compound-specific limit. For fixed-dose combinations, apply the limits to each active ingredient separately.

M7 control options: (1) test in the drug substance specification at or below the acceptable limit; (2) test in a raw material, starting material or intermediate specification, or as an in-process control, at or below the acceptable limit; (3) test upstream at a higher limit, supported by demonstrated fate and purge; (4) rely on process understanding of fate and purge without routine testing, when the scientific justification is sufficient.

M7 applies during clinical development, and the mutagenic-impurity assessment is expected to grow as development proceeds. For Phase 1 trials of 14 days or less, mitigation focuses on Class 1 and Class 2 impurities and the cohort of concern; impurities with no structural alert or in Class 3 may be treated as non-mutagenic for such short exposures. For Phase 1 trials longer than 14 days and for Phase 2a, Class 3 impurities that require analytical control should also be addressed.

Less-than-lifetime acceptable intakes may be used for clinical trials, where benefit is not yet established, as well as for marketed products, based on the expected treatment duration for most patients. For intermittent dosing, the total number of dosing days, not the calendar treatment span, sets the duration category (e.g., once-weekly dosing for two years is 104 dosing days, i.e., the 20 µg/day category).
If a mutagenic impurity has a compound-specific AI or PDE in the M7(R2) Addendum (e.g., acrylonitrile, aniline, benzyl chloride, formaldehyde), use that value instead of the TTC-based default.

No ICH-harmonised N-nitrosamine acceptable-intake framework is in force. N-nitrosamines are in the M7 cohort of concern, so the generic TTC does not apply. An M7 N-nitrosamine addendum (future M7(R3)) has been in development since June 2024; until it is adopted, nitrosamine AIs and risk-assessment expectations (e.g., the Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach) come from regional authorities.

A sponsor must submit a Clinical Trial Notification (治験計画届) to the MHLW Minister (processed by PMDA) before asking a medical institution to conduct a clinical trial of a drug. Japan uses a notification system, not an approval system.

requirements.phase: first CTN for a drug (typically phase 1)
requirements.statement: After the first CTN for a drug (初回届), the sponsor may not request the trial or contract sites until 30 days have passed. PMDA completes its review of the first CTN, including any requested document amendments, within those 30 calendar days, so sites can be contracted from day 31.

The CTN form must give these IMP particulars: identification code or name, ingredients and quantities (成分及び分量), dosage form, route of administration, the name and address of each IMP manufacturing site, and the planned quantity of IMP to be supplied.

The CTN is filed with these attachments: the document stating why the trial is judged scientifically justified (治験の実施を科学的に正当と判断した理由), the protocol, the investigator's brochure (治験薬概要書), informed-consent materials and a CRF template. Japan does not require a CTD Module 3 or IMPD-format quality dossier at CTN; quality information is summarised in the IB and the justification document.

Before requesting a trial, the sponsor must have completed the quality, toxicity and pharmacology studies of the investigational drug, and any other studies needed to request the trial (J-GCP Art. 5; article number not verified).

The sponsor must prepare an investigator's brochure (治験薬概要書) and revise it as new information emerges (J-GCP Art. 8; not verified). It must contain the chemical name or identification code of the investigational drug, information on its quality, toxicity, pharmacological action and other properties, and clinical results where they exist.

IMP containers and packaging must be labelled in Japanese with: a statement that the product is for clinical trial use, the sponsor's name and address, the chemical name or identification code, the lot (manufacturing) number, and storage conditions and expiry where these must be set. Labels and accompanying documents must not show the planned brand name, the expected indications, or the expected dosage and administration (J-GCP Art. 16; not verified).

The sponsor must supply sites only with IMP manufactured at facilities with appropriate premises, manufacturing control and quality control (J-GCP Art. 17; not verified). For drugs, the expected standard is Investigational Product GMP (治験薬GMP, notification 薬食発第0709002号 of 2008-07-09; identifier not verified).

治験薬GMP is applied in a phase-appropriate way. Process and analytical-method validation or verification is built up step by step as development progresses, and the level of control should match the development stage.

Under 治験薬GMP the sponsor must keep manufacturing and quality-control records and retention samples for each IMP lot. The documentation must be enough to compare the IMP with the eventual commercial product, so that consistency of quality can be shown later.
IMP manufactured outside Japan must be made to a standard equivalent to 治験薬GMP. The sponsor should hold evidence of this, such as audit reports or GMP certification of the foreign site.

A change to a notified CTN item, such as an IMP manufacturing site or a formulation item stated in the CTN, must be reported to PMDA in a CTN change notification (治験計画変更届). Completion and discontinuation of the trial must also be notified.

Raw materials of human or animal origin used in manufacture, such as cell substrates, serum and TSE-relevant ruminant materials, must comply with the Standard for Biological Ingredients (生物由来原料基準, MHLW Notification No. 210 of 2003, as revised; identifier not verified). How and whether compliance is formally assessed for investigational products at the CTN stage was not verified.

A gene therapy or other IMP that is a living modified organism, such as a viral vector, needs Cartagena Act clearance before it is used in a clinical trial. This means approval of Type 1 use regulations, or confirmation of containment measures for Type 2 use.

CMC questions such as specifications, stability, manufacturing changes, comparability and control strategy can be taken to PMDA in face-to-face consultations (対面助言), including drug quality consultations (医薬品品質相談). Using PMDA consultations, especially from early development, is associated with shorter and less variable later review times. Fees, menu names and the form of official records were not verified.

Each product needs manufacturing/marketing approval (製造販売承認, PMD Act Art. 14). The approval application form (承認申請書) must state, among other items, the ingredients and quantities, the manufacturing method (製造方法), dosage and administration, indications, storage method and shelf life, and the specifications and test methods (規格及び試験方法). Once approved, these entries become legally binding approved matters.

A new active ingredient application must attach two quality data categories, among others: ロ, covering manufacturing method and specifications/test methods (structure determination, physicochemical properties, manufacturing, specifications and test methods); and ハ, covering stability (long-term, stress/severe and accelerated). The data needed for each application category are set out in the 2014 MHLW notification 医薬品の承認申請について (identifier not verified).
New drug applications must be compiled in ICH CTD format (Modules 1–5) as implemented by the MHLW CTD notification. Module 3 follows ICH M4Q, and Module 2.3 (QOS) summarises it.

The Japanese Module 1 contains regional items, including: a copy of the approval application form, certificates, patent status, origin and development history (起原又は発見の経緯及び開発の経緯), foreign use status, a list of similar drugs, a draft package insert, documents on the nonproprietary name, data for poisonous or powerful drug designation, a draft RMP, and a list of attached data.
The approval application form, Module 1 and Module 2, including the 2.3 Quality Overall Summary, must be in Japanese. Modules 3–5 may be submitted in English.

The 製造方法 field of the application form must describe each manufacturing site and the process steps, process parameters, in-process controls and controls of critical steps and intermediates. Since 2005 (notification 0210001 of 2005-02-10), each entry carries symbols/annotations that fix, at approval, whether a later change needs partial change approval or only a minor change notification. The classification is settled during PMDA review, and Japan has no separate post-approval change classification guideline like those of the US and EU. Decide it during Module 3 authoring, because it fixes the post-approval change burden.

The 規格及び試験方法 field must state the specifications and analytical procedures for the drug product, and for the drug substance where it is not covered by an MF registration or a JP monograph. Where a Japanese Pharmacopoeia monograph applies, it is cited and must be met. MHLW issued a further notification on how this column and changes to it are written on 2021-07-30 (identifier not verified).

A manufacturer of a drug substance, intermediate, excipient or container/closure material may register it in the Japanese Master File (原薬等登録原簿, PMD Act Art. 80-6) to protect confidential information. The product applicant cites the MF registration number and needs a contract with the MF holder. A foreign MF holder must appoint an in-country caretaker (原薬等国内管理人).

Changes to MF-registered matters are filed by the MF holder as an MF change registration or an MF minor change notification. The MF holder must inform the MAHs whose products cite the MF, so they can assess whether their own approved matters are affected.

A drug listed in the Japanese Pharmacopoeia must conform to the current JP monograph, General Notices and General Tests. Selling a non-conforming JP drug is prohibited (PMD Act Art. 56; not verified). JP18 was still the edition cited in literature through mid-2026; whether JP19 had been promulgated by 2026-10-04 was not established. Revisions and supplements apply after their transition periods, so specifications must be kept current.

Commercial drug manufacturing sites must comply with the GMP Ministerial Ordinance (MHLW Ordinance No. 179 of 2004). Its 2021 amendment, recalled as effective 2021-08-01, added a pharmaceutical quality system, a QA unit, supplier management and data-reliability provisions. A GMP conformity inspection (GMP適合性調査) is needed at approval and periodically afterwards, recalled as every five years. None of these details were verified.

Each foreign site that manufactures a drug substance or drug product for the Japanese market must be accredited by MHLW as an accredited foreign manufacturer (外国製造業者認定, PMD Act Art. 13-3; not verified). The accreditation number is referenced for each site in the application form.

A change to an approved matter, including the manufacturing method or the specifications and test methods, needs partial change approval (一部変更承認, 一変) before it is implemented, unless it falls within the minor-change scope defined by Enforcement Regulations Art. 47.

Minor changes are filed by minor change notification (軽微変更届) within 30 days after the change (timing not verified). A change is minor only if it is not one of the types excluded by Enforcement Regulations Art. 47. The excluded types include: manufacturing-method changes that affect the product's nature, characteristics or safety; deletion or relaxation of specifications; changes to pathogen inactivation or removal methods; changes to dosage or indications; and other changes that may affect quality, efficacy or safety. Art. 47's role is corroborated; the list wording is not.

Since the 2019 PMD Act amendment, an MAH can obtain MHLW/PMDA confirmation of a change plan (変更計画, Japan's statutory PACMP mechanism, recalled as Art. 14-7-2) for quality-related approved matters. A change carried out as the confirmed plan describes can then be made by notification instead of partial change approval. The article number, effective date and notification timing were not verified.

ICH Q12 has applied in Japan since 2021. Q12 established conditions are approved matters and are stated in the approval application form as before. An EC change reported by minor change notification must still fall within Enforcement Regulations Art. 47. EC/change-category information goes in the application, and the PLCM includes the PACMP. Japan's pre-existing annotation system for approved matters is treated as equivalent to ECs. A notification of 2024-09-30 allowing risk-based post-approval changes was reported (PMID 40839206); its identifier and implementing guidelines were not established.

MHLW, PMDA and the prefectural GMP inspectorates are PIC/S Participating Authorities. Japan applied in March 2012; accession is recalled as effective 2014-07-01, not verified. Accession required the inspectorate to meet PIC/S requirements, including a quality system and access to ISO 17025 OMCLs. Membership does not by itself make the PIC/S GMP Guide legally binding in Japan; the binding standard is the Japanese GMP ordinance.

MHLW/PMDA are founding ICH regulatory members and implement ICH Quality guidelines through MHLW notifications; for example, ICH Q12 has applied in Japan since 2021. A Module 3 written to ICH M4Q and the implemented ICH Q guidelines is the expected basis for Japanese CMC review. Japanese implementation status and dates for the newest Q guidelines (e.g. Q2(R2), Q14, the Q1 revision) were not verified.

Since November 2014 the PMD Act has regulated cell and gene therapy products as a separate category, regenerative medical products (再生医療等製品), rather than as drugs. They can receive conditional, time-limited approval followed by re-review. The Act on the Safety of Regenerative Medicine, in force from the same date, separately governs regenerative medicine provided by medical institutions. Confirm the product's classification before preparing the Japanese CTN and CMC package. The GMP-equivalent standard for these products (GCTP) was not verified here.

For gene therapy products, Japanese quality and safety expectations are set out in the notification cited as No. 0709-2 on ensuring the quality and safety of gene therapy products. They include controls on adventitious agents and human-derived materials, qualification of biological raw materials used in potency assays, and biodistribution. Check the current version before preparing gene therapy CTN quality information.

Before a clinical trial of a drug starts in Korea, MFDS must approve the clinical trial plan (임상시험계획 승인, Korean IND; system introduced December 2002), and IRB approval is also required. The trial must follow KGCP. A trial of an MFDS-approved drug within its approved indication is exempt from IND approval but still needs IRB approval. Unlike Japan's CTN, this is a prior approval granted trial by trial. The legal basis is recalled as Pharmaceutical Affairs Act Art. 34 (not verified).

The Korean IND must include manufacturing and quality data for the investigational product: the active pharmaceutical ingredient and its amount, the manufacturing method, the manufacturer, the standard test methods (specifications), and quality-control results. Not confirmed: whether stability data and CTD/IMPD-style structuring are explicitly required, and how requirements scale by phase.

The IND must include documents showing the investigational product is manufactured under GMP, so that consistent batches can be produced and supplied. Not verified: the specific KGMP standard for investigational products (believed to be an annex to the Regulations on Safety of Pharmaceuticals and/or MFDS GMP rules), and the evidence accepted for IMPs made outside Korea.
Changes to an approved clinical trial plan, including changes to IMP manufacturing or quality information, need MFDS change approval. Items classed as minor need only a change report. Not verified.
MFDS's review period from IND submission to the first supplementary-data notice is 30 working days (as described in 2020). IND review and IRB review may run in parallel to shorten start-up.

IMP labels must be in Korean, must state that the product is for clinical trial use (임상시험용), and must carry the other prescribed particulars, including lot number and storage conditions/expiry. Not verified against the KGCP text.

The Korean IND package comprises: protocol; investigator's brochure; manufacturing and quality data; nonclinical pharmacology and toxicology data (toxicology and safety pharmacology from GLP-certified facilities, with GLP compliance documents); prior clinical experience; information on the institution, investigator and CRO; informed consent form; rules for compensating injured subjects; GMP compliance documents for the IMP; and a development plan covering at least the current and following year. Trials must be run at MFDS-designated clinical trial institutions. Investigator-initiated INDs for previously approved drugs may omit the IB, nonclinical data, prior clinical data and development plan if they provide supporting literature.

Korea's Advanced Regenerative Bio Act was enacted August 2019 and implemented 2020. Under it, manufacturers and importers of advanced biopharmaceuticals (cell therapy, gene therapy, tissue-engineered and advanced bio-convergence products) must be licensed by MFDS and must control every step from cell collection through testing, processing and storage. A record-management room is required for manufacturing and import permits.

A business that collects, imports, tests, processes or supplies human cells used as raw materials for advanced biopharmaceuticals needs an MFDS human-cell management licence, and donor suitability assessment is mandatory. Clinical trials of advanced biopharmaceuticals still follow the Pharmaceutical Affairs Act IND route. Products MFDS designates are subject to long-term follow-up, with sales/supply and adverse-reaction reporting.

Product approval (품목허가), recalled as under Pharmaceutical Affairs Act Art. 31, needs quality data. For new drugs it is submitted in CTD format (Module 1 Korea-specific; Modules 2–5 per ICH M4) under the MFDS Regulation on Approval, Notification and Review of Pharmaceuticals. Not verified.

Before approval, each drug substance and drug product manufacturing site, overseas sites included, must pass MFDS's KGMP compliance evaluation, which may be an on-site inspection or a document assessment. Not verified.
MFDS is a PIC/S Participating Authority (recalled as effective 2014-07-01, not verified), and KGMP is understood to be aligned with the PIC/S GMP Guide.

MFDS has been an ICH Regulatory Member since November 2016 (one secondary source) and implements ICH guidelines into MFDS guidance. ICH-compliant CTD Module 3 content is the expected basis for Korean CMC review. Which ICH Q guidelines MFDS has implemented, and when, was not verified.

Clinical trials with all or part of the clinical development in Brazil for registration purposes require a DDCM plus at least one DEEC, filed with Anvisa under RDC 945/2024, reported in force since 2025-01-01, which replaced RDC 9/2015.
Post-marketing (phase IV) and non-interventional trials are reported to be exempt from Anvisa review under RDC 945/2024. They need only research-ethics committee (CEP) approval.

The DDCM must include the DPI/IMPD (RDC 945/2024, Art. 28). Drug-substance part, as summarised from the official text: API description, nomenclature and structure; manufacturing process and in-process controls; characterization including impurities; API quality control including analytical method validation; reference standards; packaging material; stability results. Confirm against the verbatim Art. 28 before filing.

Drug-product part of the DPI/IMPD, as summarised from RDC 945/2024 Art. 28: dosage form and composition, pharmaceutical development, manufacturing process and in-process controls, excipient quality control, and investigational-medicine quality control. The summary does not mention reference standards, container closure or stability of the investigational medicine; check the verbatim Art. 28 before leaving them out.
Anvisa recommends organizing the DPI/IMPD in the CTD Module 3 structure (ICH M4) to make technical review easier (non-binding Q&A).

For reliance-based optimized review, the DPI/IMPD version submitted to Anvisa must be identical to the version approved by at least one listed AREE (IN 338/2024 as amended by IN 345/2025). Check the current AREE list in the consolidated text.

Under the optimized review, Anvisa analyses only the DPI/IMPD information on the modifications made for: products registered in Brazil or by an AREE, products modified for the trial (e.g., blinded comparators), and fixed-dose combinations.

In IN 345/2025, Anvisa said it would issue a further act or guidance detailing the DPI/IMPD quality requirements of RDC 945/2024 Art. 28. Its publication was not confirmed as of 2026-10-04. Until it is, check the DDCM/DEEC manual and the legacy quality manuals (written under RDC 9/2015) for current expectations.

Reported in secondary sources only: Anvisa reviews primary DDCM/DEEC petitions within 90 working days. Without a decision in that period, the DDCM/DEEC is released by lapse of time through a Resolução-RE in the DOU, and the trial may start after ethics approval. Check the verbatim RDC 945/2024 text, including any product categories excluded from tacit release, before relying on this.
Anvisa analyses a DDCM only once at least one DEEC is filed. The DEEC must be filed within 15 working days of the DDCM document being issued.
Substantial modifications to the investigational product after authorization are secondary petitions to Anvisa. They are eligible for optimized (reliance or risk-based) review under IN 338/2024.
RDC 945/2024 allows partial data to be submitted continuously, as they are generated, before the definitive DDCM submission.

The sponsor must ensure the investigational medicine, any modified active comparator and any placebo are made under GMP. They must be coded and labelled to protect blinding where applicable and to identify them as investigational products.

Investigational medicines made for Brazilian trials must meet the general GMP of RDC 658/2022 plus IN 136/2022, which adopts the PIC/S GMP guideline for investigational medicines as complementary requirements.

Registration of synthetic and semi-synthetic new, innovative, generic and similar medicines falls under RDC 753/2022 (which revoked RDC 200/2017), within the general framework of RDC 948/2024 (in force 2025-01-01). Quality documentation is required in the technical dossier.

Anvisa recommends the CTD format for registration and post-registration dossiers (Guia 24). Version 1 (2019-08-14) made CTD optional. Version 2 (dated 2026-04-25, published 2026-05-04) is in effect and open for comment until 2026-11-04; whether it makes CTD mandatory is unconfirmed.

APIs used in new, innovative, generic and similar medicines go through Anvisa's DIFA dossier and CADIFA adequacy letter under RDC 359/2020. Guia 24 v2 is reported to fold the CADIFA flow into the CTD format.

Biological products are registered under RDC 55/2010, within the general framework of RDC 948/2024. RDC 55/2010 is reported to remain in force as complemented and amended in 2024; check the consolidated text for any provisions those amendments revoked.

To run a clinical trial of a new drug or IND, apply to the Central Licensing Authority on Form CT-04, with the Second Schedule information and the Sixth Schedule fee. Permission is granted on Form CT-06 (NDCT Rules 2019).

Among other items, the Second Schedule's chemical and pharmaceutical information covers: chemical, code and generic name; structure; physicochemical properties; dosage form with qualitative and quantitative composition (actives and excipients); specifications of active and inactive ingredients with pharmacopoeial references; and the active ingredient's source. This list is a paraphrase from summaries and may be incomplete; read the Second Schedule item in full before filing.
Submit identification tests for the active ingredients, assay methods, and impurity-profile tests with reference standards for the impurities (NDCT Rules 2019, Second Schedule).

Stability data, both accelerated and real-time, are required. For India (zone IVb), the conditions cited are long-term 30 ± 2 °C / 75 ± 5% RH and accelerated 40 ± 2 °C / 75 ± 5% RH for 6 months. These conditions come from summaries of the Second Schedule and the WHO zone definition; check the Gazette text.

CDSCO decides a CT-04 application within 90 working days. Drugs discovered or developed in India and to be manufactured and marketed there have a 30-working-day route, and only on that route is silence past the deadline deemed approval. The 2026 amendments shortened test-licence timelines; any change to the CT-04 timeline itself is unconfirmed.

Manufacturing a new drug or IND for trials needs permission: apply on CT-10; permission is granted on CT-11, valid 3 years. Importing one for trials needs an application on CT-16. Since G.S.R. 46(E) (2026-01-20), the statutory timeline under rules 53 and 60 is reported as 45 working days instead of 90.

Since the 2026 amendment, a new drug or IND made only for analytical or non-clinical testing can be produced after an online prior intimation to CDSCO, without a test licence. Exceptions that still need permission: sex hormones, cytotoxics, beta-lactams, biologics with live microorganisms, narcotics and psychotropics.

Indian manufacturers must comply with revised Schedule M (G.S.R. 922(E), 2023-12-28), which requires a pharmaceutical quality system, quality risk management, product quality review, and qualification and validation. It includes a dedicated part on manufacturing investigational pharmaceutical products for human clinical trials.

Revised Schedule M has applied to manufacturers with turnover above Rs 250 crore since 2024-06-28. Smaller manufacturers had a conditional extension to 2025-12-31 (G.S.R. 127(E), 2025-02-11). Since 2026-01-01, it applies to all manufacturers, small and large.

Marketing approval of a new drug needs an application on Form CT-18 (import) or CT-21 (manufacture), as API or formulation, with Second Schedule data. CDSCO's 2010 CTD guidance sets out the five-module format, with Module 3 for quality.
Quality information for biotechnological and biological new-drug applications follows CDSCO's 2008 Guidance for Industry. Its current status after the NDCT Rules 2019 is unconfirmed.

Broadly: trials of therapeutic products or Class 2 CTGTPs need a CTA where the product is unregistered locally or used outside its approved label. A CTN is the route for locally registered products used within the approved label. Trials of medicinal products under the Medicines Act need a CTC. All are filed on PRISM. Check GN-IOCTB-04 for the exact eligibility criteria for CTN.

Submit a GMP certificate for the finished-product manufacturer of every locally unregistered investigational and auxiliary product. Without one, submit a declaration that the product is made under current GMP and sourced from an authorised manufacturer in the country of origin.
For biologics and Class 2 CTGTPs, also submit the GMP certificate of the drug-substance manufacturer.
Submit certificates of analysis for the study batches of investigational products with the CTA or CTN.
HSA does not routinely require full CMC data for therapeutic-product CTAs; CMC information is submitted when HSA requests it.
For Class 2 CTGTP trials and registration, the CMC dossier must detail starting-material origin, reagent quality, manufacturing process and controls, analytical methods, and stability (GN-ATPB-1-4).

HSA target review times, excluding stop-clock time: CTA 30 working days (15 for phase 1 BA/BE, food-effect or DDI trials; 60 for Class 2 CTGTP trials); CTN 5 working days; substantial amendments 15 working days (CTA/CTC) or 5 (CTN).

Importers must file a Clinical Research Materials notification before importing CRM, unless the material is locally registered and they are its licensed importer. The notification is valid one year and must remain valid while the CRM is imported or supplied.

Under HSA's labelling guidance, investigational and auxiliary product labels must protect participants and allow product tracking, identify the product and trial, support correct use and storage, and protect data reliability.

Since 2021-03-01, CTGTPs in Singapore have been regulated under the Health Products Act (Health Products (CTGTP) Regulations 2021), not the Medicines Act. They are classed as lower-risk Class 1 or moderate- to higher-risk Class 2 by degree of manipulation, intended use, and combination with therapeutic products or devices. Classify the product first: the clinical-trial route and CMC expectations depend on the class.

Therapeutic-product registration dossiers must be in English and in either ICH CTD format (quality in Module 3) or ACTD format (quality in Part II). The chosen format cannot be changed after submission.
Since 2026-04-01, HSA has accepted eCTD dossiers on a voluntary basis (ICH eCTD v3.2.2, SG-HSA regional spec v1.1).
Reported in secondary sources only: since 2026-06-01, applicants must declare that the submitted CMC dossier contains no known quality defects needing update.

Under WHO's standard, investigational products must be manufactured, packaged, tested, handled, stored and distributed under an effective quality management system and applicable GMP, per TRS 1044 Annex 7 (2022), which replaced TRS 863 Annex 7 (1996).

Novel radiopharmaceuticals without marketing authorization, prepared for phase I–III investigations, should meet the minimum GMP standards of the IAEA/WHO guideline on GMP for investigational radiopharmaceutical products (reported as TRS 1044 Annex 3, 2022; confirm the annex title).

Stability data for APIs and FPPs should follow TRS 1010 Annex 10 (2018). Long-term conditions depend on the target climatic zone: 30 °C/65% RH for zone IVa and 30 °C/75% RH for zone IVb. Accelerated testing is 40 °C/75% RH for 6 months.

For WHO prequalification of generic FPPs, organize the quality part per ICH M4Q (CTD-Quality): a Quality Overall Summary (Module 2.3) and Module 3 data (TRS 970 Annex 4). National regulators use the parallel TRS 986 Annex 6 guideline, which applies the same structure with WHO API/FPP terms.
WHO prequalification follows the procedure in TRS 1067 Annex 4, published 2026-06-09, which is presumed to replace the 2011 procedure in TRS 961.

PIC/S GMP Guide Annex 13 (Manufacture of Investigational Medicinal Products) was revised to align with the EU framework under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. It has applied since 2022-02-01 (PE 009-16). Participating Authorities apply it through their own national instruments; ANVISA, for example, adopted the PIC/S IMP GMP guideline via IN 136/2022. Do not assume every PIC/S member applies Annex 13 directly: the EU applies C(2017) 8179, and other members have their own IMP GMP rules.

Keep a Product Specification File holding all reference documents needed to make the IMP to GMP and to the clinical-trial authorization (PIC/S Annex 13). Whether Annex 13 states that the applicable sections must exist before the first batch was not verified verbatim.

In PIC/S terminology, IMP batches are certified for release by an Authorised Person (equivalent to the EU Qualified Person), under the release provisions of revised Annex 13. Annex 16 (Certification by the Authorised Person and Batch Release) was introduced in the same PE 009-16 revision.
The current PIC/S GMP Guide is PE 009-18 (in force 2026-09-24). Its only change is a revised Annex 19, so Annex 13 is unchanged from PE 009-16/-17.

In the EU, IMP GMP rests on Delegated Regulation (EU) 2017/1569 and the Detailed Commission guideline C(2017) 8179, both applicable since the CTR began to apply (2022-01-31). Since the CTR transition ended (2025-01-30), they cover all EU trials.
