notes.topic: What does a Q2(R2) validation study need that a Q2(R1) study did not?
notes.phase: phase 2-3 / marketing (principles usable phase-appropriately at phase 1)
notes.summary: Q2(R2) expects confidence-interval limits for accuracy and precision to be compatible with the acceptance criteria, unless otherwise justified. It also allows prior knowledge, such as development data or earlier studies, to support the validation conclusion. Robustness is now evaluated during development, consistent with Q14; Q2(R2) Annex II gives technique-specific examples. Q2(R2) also covers platform analytical procedures, which can justify reduced product-specific validation. Plan the statistics, such as interval estimates, into the protocol before execution.
keyPoints: Q2(R2) adds a statement that confidence-interval limits for accuracy and precision should be compatible with acceptance criteria, unless otherwise justified [PMID:41299187; PMID:39966106].

Q2(R2) allows prior knowledge (development data, previous studies) to support validation conclusions. Faya et al. give frequentist and Bayesian ways to combine prior knowledge with validation results [PMID:41299187].
Robustness belongs to development under Q2(R2)/Q14. An FDA laboratory evaluated MS parameter extremes and treated the accepted ranges as potential proven acceptable ranges [PMID:39111548].

Q2(R2) Annex II examples include multiple MRM transitions with a quantifier/qualifier ratio criterion for specificity, and stable-isotope internal standards to control matrix effects in MS procedures [PMID:39111548].
Platform validation data can be used when a platform analytical procedure is applied to a new product, with project-specific work limited to specificity [PMID:39966106; PMID:41936258].
NOT verified this session: Q2(R2) wording on 'reportable range'/'working range' and on combined accuracy-precision evaluation. Check against the guideline text before citing.
commonDeficiencies: No retrieved regulator analysis isolates Q2(R2)-specific deficiencies. EU IMPD deficiency letters most often cite inadequately justified or incomplete specifications. Specifications rest on validated methods [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].

notes.topic: What is the Q14 enhanced approach, and how does analytical development data earn post-approval flexibility through Established Conditions?
notes.summary: Under Q14, development can follow a minimal or an enhanced approach, with a continuum between them. Enhanced elements include an analytical target profile (ATP), evaluation of prior knowledge, risk assessment, a defined analytical procedure control strategy and lifecycle change management. Development and validation data can justify which procedure parameters are Established Conditions (ECs) and the reporting category for changing each one. In the US, these proposals may differ from the default categories in 21 CFR 314.70 or 601.12. FDA authors have published worked examples of EC proposals for analytical procedures. They note that the full potential of Q12/Q14 remains unrealised because sponsors are unsure how development data translate into flexibility.
keyPoints: Enhanced-approach elements include identifying an ATP, evaluating prior and gained knowledge, conducting a risk assessment and defining the control strategy [PMID:39111548; PMID:39704537].

The ATP states the intended purpose and the required performance (e.g., a 0.1 ppm quantitation limit driven by an acceptable-intake limit). FDA authors used the 'Sakuratinib' example in ICH Q14 section 13.1.1 as their template [PMID:39111548].

The analytical procedure control strategy covers system suitability before and after runs, sample suitability (e.g., IS-normalised matrix effect 90–110%, CV <15%) and ongoing performance monitoring [PMID:39111548].
ECs for analytical procedures can include method parameters, operational conditions and acceptance criteria. They may be parameter-based or, with more experience, performance-based [PMID:39111548].
In the US, applicants may propose ECs and reporting categories that differ from 21 CFR 314.70/601.12 and the change guidances, justified by risk management and development data [PMID:39111548].
FDA OPQ published a case study showing how to determine, propose and justify analytical ECs and reporting categories, identify non-EC elements, and present them in a submission [PMID:40087229].
An industry framework stresses balancing the benefit of post-approval flexibility against the resources needed for enhanced elements [PMID:39704537].
commonDeficiencies: FDA authors report uncertainty over how development data can be used to gain flexibility, which keeps Q12/Q14 uptake low [PMID:40087229].
Most early EC proposals are parameter-based rather than performance-based, which limits flexibility [PMID:39111548].

notes.topic: How much analytical method validation is expected for a phase 1 IND/IMPD versus phase 2-3 and marketing?
notes.summary: US IND regulations scale CMC information to the phase. An initial phase 1 IND emphasises identifying and controlling raw materials and the drug substance; final specifications are not expected until the end of development (21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)). Industry practice is a phase-appropriate validation following Q2(R2) principles before release of first-in-human material. Biologic and ATMP potency or cytotoxicity assays are often qualified for phase 1/2a and fully validated before pivotal studies. FDA has long described specifications and assay validation as tightening in stages from IND to licensure. EU expectations for phase I validation documentation in the IMPD come from EMA's IMP quality guidelines; their wording and identifiers were not verified in this session.
keyPoints: 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7): the amount of CMC information needed to assure identity, quality, purity and strength varies with phase, trial duration, dosage form and other available information. A phase 1 IND should emphasise identification and control of raw materials and drug substance (regulation text paraphrased; eCFR not fetched this session).

Platform methods with phase-appropriate validation per ICH Q2(R2) support first-in-human biologic INDs. MSD reports a typical FIH validation took up to 4 months before platform validation [PMID:39966106].

Cell-therapy potency methods can be qualified against predefined acceptance criteria for accuracy, precision, linearity, range, specificity, robustness and carryover for a phase I/IIa trial, then advanced to validation for pivotal studies [PMID:38304826].

FDA (CBER) described specification setting as phased: practical operational limits early, then assay validation and refinement during clinical development, and tighter specifications at licensure [PMID:9413677].
Small-molecule impurity control distinguishes phase-appropriate profiling and stress testing from fully validated, stability-indicating methods later [DOI:10.1007/s11095-026-04054-y].

EU IMPD: EMA's chemical and biological IMP quality guidelines set phase-dependent validation documentation (recalled: method suitability confirmed and parameters/acceptance limits tabulated for phase I; tabulated validation results later). NOT verified this session. Confirm against the current EMA text.
commonDeficiencies: FDA-listed CGT CMC deficiencies leading to clinical holds include inadequate potency assays and release specifications [PMID:37886603].
Chinese CDE rejections of ATMP INDs included failure to properly perform safety testing such as replication-competent lentivirus testing [PMID:37125239].
EU IMPD deficiency letters most often cite inadequately justified or incomplete specifications and insufficient stability data [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].

notes.topic: Can platform analytical procedures and historical validation data shorten validation for a first-in-human biologic IND?
notes.summary: For modality-independent release methods, a sponsor can pool historical validation data, then run a feasibility check and a limited product-specific validation for a new molecule. Examples are protein concentration, polysorbate 80, L-methionine, SEC, CE-SDS, residual HCP and residual Protein A. MSD's workflow uses at least 3 historical validations and 99% prediction intervals to show that future accuracy and precision will meet early-phase criteria; the new validation then tests only specificity. Validation time fell from up to 4 months to 1–2 months, and the approach was used in FIH IND filings. The platform must have defined boundaries; outside its validated range, product-specific development and validation are required.
keyPoints: Prerequisite is sufficient historical validation data (≥3 validations) for the same platform method [PMID:39966106].

Pooled accuracy (% recovery) and precision (%RSD) are analysed with a linear mixed model. 99% prediction intervals for future results are compared with early-clinical acceptance criteria [PMID:39966106].
Project-specific validation can be limited to specificity (lack of interference), after a feasibility test of accuracy and precision at the target level [PMID:39966106].
Prediction intervals are wider than confidence intervals. If they meet the criteria, the Q2(R2) confidence-interval expectation is considered satisfied [PMID:39966106; PMID:41299187].

Boundaries matter. For example, a PS-80 platform validated for 0.05–0.35 mg/mL needs re-evaluation below that range. Non-suitable products revert to product-specific, phase-appropriate validation [PMID:39966106].
An IABS workshop (2025, published 2026) with EMA, EDQM, CBG-MEB and FDA participants stressed clearly defined platform boundaries and applicability, and early dialogue with reviewers [PMID:41936258].
commonDeficiencies: Platform claims without defined applicability boundaries were identified as a key concern in regulator–industry discussion [PMID:41936258].

notes.topic: When an analytical procedure changes between clinical phases or after approval, what bridging and ongoing monitoring is expected?
notes.summary: Under Q14 lifecycle principles, a change within proven ranges is low risk but still needs a bridging study. The study should show the revised procedure meets its validation criteria and gives data comparable with the original procedure. Changing the technology or detection mode means repeating the risk assessment, redeveloping and revalidating against the ATP. Routine data should feed continued performance verification of bias and precision. Legacy methods should be checked periodically for robustness to reagent, consumable and supplier changes. For CGT products, inadequate potency assays and comparability bridging are among FDA's listed CMC reasons for clinical holds.
keyPoints: Post-approval changes to procedure parameters need bridging studies showing the revised method meets validation criteria and gives data comparable to the original [PMID:39111548].
A change of technique (e.g., MS mode or acquisition algorithm) triggers a new risk assessment, re-development and re-validation to the ATP [PMID:39111548].
Continued verification of bias and precision, as in USP <1220> and advocated in Q14, can be done by estimating method variability from routine results [PMID:39053096].
Analytical method lifecycle management is commonly framed as three stages: method design, method performance qualification and continued method performance verification [PMID:33835304].

Robustness re-evaluation of a legacy N-glycan method found different PNGase F enzyme sources, SPE cartridges and labelling-reagent stability affected results. These are lifecycle risks to control [PMID:41562782].
The analytical procedure control strategy should secure supply of critical reagents. One study identified alternative background-electrolyte components for a mAb CZE method [PMID:40988426].
FDA-listed CGT CMC hold triggers include development of adequate potency assays and comparability bridging studies [PMID:37886603].
commonDeficiencies: Inadequate potency assay development and missing comparability bridging were typical CMC deficiencies leading to CGT clinical holds [PMID:37886603].
Toxicology batches not comparable with clinical batches were a reason Chinese CDE rejected ATMP INDs [PMID:37125239].

notes.topic: What are ICH Q12 Established Conditions, when are they proposed, and which regions accept them today?
notes.phase: marketing (plan the supporting development data during phase 2-3)
notes.summary: ICH Q12 reached Step 4 on 20 November 2019. It provides three tools: Established Conditions (ECs), post-approval change management protocols (PACMPs) and the Product Lifecycle Management (PLCM) document. ECs are the CMC elements needed to assure product quality, and changing them requires regulatory action. Q12 addresses the commercial phase, so ECs are proposed in marketing applications or post-approval submissions, not in INDs or CTAs. Clinical-phase QbD and enhanced development work decides how far ECs can later be justified. As of the ICH website on 17 June 2024, Q12 was implemented by FDA (May 2021) and PMDA (October 2021), with an NMPA pilot from August 2023. The EU lacked a legal basis for ECs at the time of a 2024 survey. Uptake in US and EU NDAs remains very low.
keyPoints: Q12 reached Step 4 on 2019-11-20 [PMID:40839206]. FDA issued the Q12 guidance in May 2021 [PMID:38545329].
Q12 'addresses the commercial phase of the product lifecycle (as described in ICH Q10)' (quoted in [PMID:40839206]). ECs, PLCM and PACMP are marketing-stage tools.

ECs are CMC elements (process, facilities and equipment, control-strategy elements) necessary to assure quality. Every application contains ECs, but they are often not explicitly identified [PMID:38545329].
ICH status at 2024-06-17: implemented by FDA (2021-05) and PMDA (2021-10); NMPA pilot initiated 2023-08; other members implementing or not started [PMID:39179719].
In the 2024 JPMA survey, US NDAs with ECs were 5/85, EU 3/107 and Japan 64/191 (2019–Apr 2024). The EU had no legal framework for ECs at the time [PMID:40839206].
Japan has used approval-matter annotations that pre-set change categories since 2005, a concept equivalent to ECs. Q12 has been effective in Japan since 2021 [PMID:40839206].
Defining ECs does not reduce data requirements for a change. It pre-agrees the reporting category [PMID:40839206].
EU status as of 2026-10 (revised Variations Regulation and guidelines enabling ECs) was NOT verified in this research.
commonDeficiencies: Sponsors avoid ECs because they are not mandatory, the concept is poorly understood internally, the benefit is unclear and they fear review delay [PMID:40839206].
In a 2023 survey of 9 selected ICH members, none had implemented ECs or the PLCM document. The US, EU, Japan, Canada and Switzerland were not among those surveyed [PMID:39179719].

notes.topic: When is a post-approval change management protocol (PACMP) worth filing, and what evidence shows it pays off?
notes.summary: A PACMP gets prior regulatory agreement on the plan, studies and acceptance criteria for a future change. The change is then implemented under a lower reporting category once the results meet the agreed criteria. Its value is greatest for changes repeated across products or markets, such as new fill lines, site transfers or new assays. Adoption across national authorities is still narrow because many need legislative changes to downgrade reporting after protocol approval. A published multi-product PACMP approved by a WHO-Listed Authority brought implementation of a new aseptic filling line, serving 5 products, forward by 7 months. It also enabled reliance-based approvals elsewhere. Science- and risk-based stability strategies can further reduce the stability data commitment or reporting category.
keyPoints: A PACMP gives prior approval of the methodology before accelerated approval of the technical results. It suits changes such as a new assay or a site change [PMID:39179719].
In the 2023 industry survey, Brazil was the only selected ICH member using PACMPs (drug substance, with a drug product pilot in 2023) [PMID:39179719].
Limited uptake is attributed to the legislative changes needed to allow a reduced classification after protocol approval [PMID:39179719].

A multi-product PACMP for an aseptic filling line serving 5 approved products, approved by a WHO-Listed Authority, accelerated implementation by 7 months and supported reliance-based approvals in other countries [PMID:41044288].
Ten case studies show prior stability knowledge can justify reduced stability commitments or lower reporting categories for CMC changes [PMID:38485849].
Global post-approval changes can take 3–5 years to approve worldwide, which is the business case for PACMPs and reliance [PMID:35917091; PMID:39179719].
Regulatory flexibility for post-approval changes assumes demonstrated PQS effectiveness (ICH Q10 Annex 1) [PMID:32467177; PMID:29669814].
commonDeficiencies: Respondents reported long, unpredictable timelines, extra local requirements and categorisation stricter than the EMA/WHO benchmark for the same change [PMID:39179719].

notes.topic: What must a dossier for a continuously manufactured drug substance or drug product show under ICH Q13?
notes.summary: ICH Q13 covers continuous manufacturing (CM) of drug substances and drug products. Its annexes include therapeutic-protein drug substance. The core dossier evidence is characterisation of process dynamics, typically residence time distribution (RTD) for each unit operation and the integrated line. RTD models then support material traceability and diversion of nonconforming material. They can also be built into the control strategy and in-process limits, as one RTD-model control strategy accepted by regulators shows. An FDA self-audit found no substantive regulatory barriers for CM applications; they reached approval faster than comparable batch applications. FDA biopharmaceutics reviewers report recurring deficiencies when CM is combined with real-time release testing for dissolution.
keyPoints: Q13 (quoted while in draft) requests understanding of process dynamics as a function of input material attributes and process conditions. A common approach is RTD characterisation for unit operations and the integrated system [PMID:36206581].
RTD-based models enable material traceability and diversion of disturbed material, including in continuous Protein A capture for biologics [PMID:41687211; PMID:36206581].
An RTD-model design space was incorporated statistically into a commercial control strategy, tightened in-process control limits, and was accepted by regulators [PMID:35214087].

In an FDA self-audit, CM applications reached approval 8 (mean) or 3 (median) months faster and market 12 or 4 months faster than similar batch applications. No substantial barriers were found for post-approval changes or pre-approval inspections [PMID:35500688].
Q13 has five annexes. Annex III addresses therapeutic-protein drug substance [PMID:40872548].

Dates: FDA adopted Q13 as guidance in March 2023 and EMA made it effective in July 2023, both per a single review (low confidence) [PMID:40872548]. A Q13 draft existed in 2022 [PMID:36206581]. ICH Step 4 date (believed November 2022) NOT verified.
Q13 batch-definition and state-of-control expectations were NOT re-verified against the guideline text in this research.
commonDeficiencies: FDA-reported deficiencies with CM plus RTRT for dissolution: inadequate stratified sampling of drug product units, inappropriate DoE, RTRT models that do not capture dissolution variability or the full time course, insufficient documentation, and unsuitable in vitro dissolution methods [PMID:37572781].

notes.topic: What changed in ICH Q9(R1), and how should quality risk management be applied and documented in a clinical-stage CMC program?
notes.summary: ICH Q9 (Quality Risk Management) was first published in 2005 and revised as Q9(R1) in January 2023. The revision added guidance on risk-based decision-making. It also makes clear that QRM supports decisions but does not remove the obligation to comply with regulatory requirements. ICH training material for Q9(R1) featured the Risk-Knowledge Infinity cycle, which links QRM to knowledge management. In development, QRM outputs appear in the dossier as justifications. Examples are criticality assessments in 3.2.P.2 and 3.2.S.2.6, impurity and nitrosamine risk assessments in 3.2.S.3.2, and specification justifications in 3.2.P.5.6. Benefits of QRM are limited by weak role-based competence.
keyPoints: Q9 was published in 2005 [PMID:31101709]. Q9 was revised in 2023 [PMID:40839206]. The revision was dated January 2023 and expanded guidance on risk-based decision-making [PMID:40032319].

Q9(R1) states that QRM can aid decision-making but does not eliminate the obligation to comply with regulatory requirements. Example: assessing alternatives to EU Annex 1 PUPSIT requires a documented risk assessment [PMID:40032319].
ICH-sanctioned Q9(R1) training featured the Risk-Knowledge Infinity cycle linking QRM and knowledge management [PMID:38942476].
Nitrosamine risk assessments by applicants and API manufacturers are expected to use ICH Q9 QRM principles [PMID:38253223].
Fourteen years after Q9, industry still struggled to realise QRM benefits; role-based QRM competencies were proposed [PMID:31101709].

NOT verified this session: the other Q9(R1) revision themes (managing subjectivity, formality, product-availability/shortage risk, hazard identification) and the exact adoption day. Confirm against the guideline text.
commonDeficiencies: Industry has not fully applied Q9 principles to assess and manage product-quality risks as a surrogate for patient safety [PMID:31101709].
No regulator deficiency statistics specific to QRM documentation in INDs/IMPDs were retrieved.

notes.topic: What quality system is expected while a product is in clinical development, and how does PQS effectiveness later earn regulatory flexibility?
notes.summary: ICH Q10 (2008) describes a pharmaceutical quality system model for every stage of the product lifecycle. In the US, a 2008 final rule exempted most phase 1 investigational drugs from the 21 CFR Part 211 CGMP regulations. FDA still oversees phase 1 manufacture under its statutory CGMP authority and through IND review, guided by the companion guidance 'CGMP for Phase 1 Investigational Drugs'. Regulations do not cover non-GMP R&D CMC laboratories. Industry authors therefore recommend a stage-appropriate R&D quality system so that development data are reliable, traceable and fit to present to regulators. At the commercial stage, demonstrated PQS effectiveness is what regulators rely on to grant Q12/Q10 Annex 1 flexibility.
keyPoints: ICH Q10 was issued in 2008 as a harmonised PQS model applicable across lifecycle stages [PMID:24265300; PMID:32999074].

US: most phase 1 investigational drugs are exempt from Part 211 CGMP requirements (final rule, 73 FR 40453, 15 July 2008). FDA oversight continues under statutory CGMP and IND review, with the companion guidance 'CGMP for Phase 1 Investigational Drugs' [PMID:18850678].
The exemption covers phase 1 only. Investigational drugs for later phases remain subject to the CGMP regulations (inferred from the rule's scope; confirm against 21 CFR 210.2) [PMID:18850678].
No regulatory guideline covers quality practices in R&D CMC laboratories running non-cGMP studies. A stage-appropriate R&D quality system protects data that may later be submitted [PMID:39313151].
Specifications for biological IMPs can be set and revised within a flexible quality system across early and late development [PMID:26429107].
Post-approval regulatory relief depends on science- and risk-based concepts plus demonstrated PQS effectiveness in maintaining a state of control [PMID:29669814; PMID:32467177].
EU and other regions: GMP for IMPs is set in regional law (e.g., EU rules under Regulation (EU) No 536/2014). The specific EU instrument and text were NOT verified this session.
commonDeficiencies: Two decades after Q8/Q9/Q10, PQS transformation was reported to be under way in only a few organisations, with most still aspiring to it [PMID:24265300].
R&D studies may lack elements needed to present the data to regulators, discovered only in hindsight [PMID:39313151].

notes.topic: How often do FDA INDs go on clinical hold for CMC reasons, and which CMC gaps trigger holds?
notes.summary: An IND takes effect 30 days after FDA receives it unless FDA imposes a clinical hold (21 CFR 312.40, 312.42). FDA's own analysis of all initial CDER INDs in FY2013 found 8.9% (125 of 1,410) placed on hold within 30 days, with CMC the most common reason. In FDA's oncology office, holds were mainly clinical, followed by pharmaceutical quality. They clustered in first-in-human INDs and sponsors with limited regulatory experience. For cell and gene therapies in 2020–2022, about a fifth of publicly announced holds were CMC-driven, and CMC holds took longest to resolve. Most CMC holds were judged avoidable by following FDA's product-specific CMC guidance and using pre-IND meetings well.
keyPoints: CDER FY2013: 1,410 initial INDs, of which 125 (8.9%) were placed on hold within 30 days. CMC was the most cited reason, then clinical, then toxicology. More than half became active within a year [PMID:26911627].
Holds did not differ substantively between rare- and common-disease INDs or between commercial and research sponsors. Many holds were avoidable by following available guidance [PMID:26911627].

FDA oncology (OHOP): under 10% of new commercial INDs were placed on hold or withdrawn in the 30-day review. Deficiencies were mainly clinical, then pharmaceutical quality, then nonclinical. Holds were concentrated in FIH trials and inexperienced sponsors [PMID:31678263].
Experienced sponsors benefited more from pre-IND meetings. Focused questions and supporting data in the meeting package are recommended [PMID:31678263].
CGT (public announcements, 2020–2022): 33 holds, 7 (21%) for CMC. Resolving holds that required additional CMC information took an average of 8.4 months [PMID:37886603].
FDA has 30 days to issue formal hold comments and 30 days to review a complete response, so at least 60 days on hold is likely [PMID:37886603].
CBER/OCTGT found the same deficiencies recurring across cell and gene therapy INDs placed on hold [PMID:18418776].
commonDeficiencies: FDA-listed CGT CMC hold triggers: compatibility with administration devices and containers; stability during transport; inadequate potency assays; comparability bridging studies; substantive manufacturing changes; release specifications [PMID:37886603].
Nonclinical (toxicology) material not shown to be representative of clinical material [PMID:37886603].
CMC was the leading reason for CDER IND holds in FY2013 [PMID:26911627].

notes.topic: Which CMC deficiencies do EU and Chinese regulators raise on clinical trial applications?
notes.summary: A retrospective analysis covered 74 deficiency letters on 26 initial EU clinical trial applications from 2015 to 2024. The most frequent IMPD findings were inadequately justified or incomplete specifications, missing or insufficient stability data, and incomplete descriptions of manufacturing controls and critical process parameters. These findings appeared for chemical, biological and ATMP products. China's CDE received 271 ATMP IND applications from 2017 to November 2022 and approved 217. Rejections cited missing essential data, raw-material safety issues, improper safety testing such as replication-competent lentivirus testing, and toxicology batches not comparable with clinical batches. Under the EU CTR, sponsors must answer requests for information within 12 days, so CMC answers must be ready to deploy.
keyPoints: EU IMPD deficiencies, 2015–2024 (74 letters, 26 trials): specifications inadequately justified or incomplete; stability data missing or insufficient; manufacturing controls and CPPs incompletely described [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
These IMPD deficiencies occurred across chemical and biological drug substances, ATMPs and multiple dosage forms [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].

China (CDE), ATMP INDs 2017–Nov 2022: 271 applications, 217 approved, 54 rejected. Reasons included lack of essential data, raw-material safety issues, improper safety testing (e.g., RCL) and toxicology-to-clinical batch incomparability [PMID:37125239].
China has suggested pre-IND meetings since 2018. CDE reports reviewer feedback in pre-IND and pre-pre-IND meetings markedly reduced IND rejection rates for ATMPs [PMID:37125239].
EU CTR permits 12 days to respond to requests for information. A non-commercial sponsor averaged 27.5 days before the CTR [PMID:37389794].
Academic ATMP developers often lack IMPD expertise. Early interaction with national competent authorities is recommended [PMID:38260921].
commonDeficiencies: Inadequately justified or incomplete specifications (EU) [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
Missing or insufficient stability data (EU) [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
Incomplete description of manufacturing controls and critical process parameters (EU) [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
Raw-material safety issues, inadequate RCL testing, and toxicology vs clinical batch incomparability (China, ATMP) [PMID:37125239].

notes.topic: How do the review models and clocks differ for a US IND, EU CTR application, Japan CTN, China IND, Health Canada CTA and Australian CTN/CTA?
notes.summary: Regulators co-authored a six-jurisdiction comparison (FDA, EMA, MHRA, Health Canada, PMDA, TGA). The US IND takes effect 30 days after receipt unless placed on hold. Health Canada reviews a completed CTA in 30 days and issues a No Objection Letter or Not Satisfactory Notice. Japan requires the first CTN for a new active ingredient at least 31 days before trial start, with a 30-day PMDA review. EU CTR applications go through CTIS; Part I, which contains the IMPD, has a coordinated 45-day assessment led by a Reporting Member State, then a 5-day decision. Australia's CTN scheme involves no TGA data evaluation, whereas the CTA scheme involves TGA safety evaluation (target 50 days) and is mandatory for high-risk biologicals. China has used an implied-licence IND system since July 2018, with a 60-day review clock.
keyPoints: US: an IND goes into effect 30 days after FDA receipt unless FDA notifies earlier or imposes a clinical hold [21 CFR 312.40; PMID:40303377].

EU CTR: one dossier via CTIS. Part I (protocol, IB, IMPD, benefit-risk) is assessed jointly by Member States Concerned, led by the Reporting Member State. Part II (ethics/national) is assessed by each state [PMID:40303377].

EU CTR clock: 45 assessment days from a valid application, then a maximum 5-day decision phase. Extended timeframes are possible for ATMPs or requests for information [PMID:40303377]. RFI responses are due within 12 days [PMID:37389794].
EU CTR transition ended 30 January 2025, so all EU trials now run under the CTR [PMID:40949130].

Japan: a CTN to MHLW (with CMC, toxicology, pharmacology and protocol) is required at least 31 days before an FIH trial of a new active ingredient, new route or new fixed combination. PMDA reviews in 30 days; other trials need 2 weeks/14 days. Most sponsors use PMDA consultation beforehand [PMID:40303377].

Canada: 30-day review from receipt of a completed CTA, ending in a No Objection Letter or a Not Satisfactory Notice. The Pharmaceutical Drugs Directorate reviews pharmaceuticals; the Biologic and Radiopharmaceutical Drugs Directorate reviews biologics, cell and gene therapies [PMID:40303377].

Australia: under the CTN scheme the TGA does not evaluate data and the HREC approves the trial (notifications processed in about 5 days). The CTA scheme involves TGA safety evaluation, has a 50-day target and is mandatory for high-risk biologicals [PMID:40303377].
China: since July 2018 an implied-licence system (NMPA No. 50, 2018) cut IND review from 90 to 60 days [PMID:37125239]. China joined ICH in 2017 [PMID:37125239].
UK (for reference): MHRA initial review maximum 30 days, or 60 days if issues must be resolved [PMID:40303377].
commonDeficiencies: CDER FY2013: 8.9% of initial INDs placed on hold in the 30-day window, most often for CMC [PMID:26911627].
EU sponsors historically took longer than the CTR's 12-day RFI window to respond (average 27.5 days at one sponsor) [PMID:37389794].

notes.topic: What must a global program plan for when one product's CMC package supports a US IND, EU CTR IMPD, Japan CTN, China IND, Health Canada CTA and Australian CTN/CTA?
notes.summary: The same Module 3-style core can serve every region, but the review gate differs. FDA uses a 30-day safety review with a phase-scaled CMC expectation. The EU IMPD sits in Part I and is assessed jointly under a 45+5-day clock with 12-day RFI windows. Japan reviews a CTN that includes CMC data in 30 days. China reviews an IND under a 60-day implied-licence clock, with heavy use of pre-IND meetings. Health Canada reviews in 30 days. Australia's CTN involves no TGA data review, but high-risk biologicals must use the TGA-evaluated CTA. Build the core dossier to the most demanding published deficiency patterns: justified specifications, adequate stability data, described CPPs and controls, raw-material safety, and tox-to-clinical batch comparability. Plan GMP evidence region by region; the US phase 1 exemption from Part 211 is a US-specific provision. Several region-specific content requirements were not verified here (see gaps), so this note is low confidence.
keyPoints: Harmonise the core CMC narrative and data to the strictest observed deficiency themes: specification justification, stability, CPP and control descriptions (EU) [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3]; raw materials, safety testing and tox/clinical batch comparability (China) [PMID:37125239]; potency, transport stability, device compatibility and comparability (US CGT) [PMID:37886603].

Sequence submissions around the clocks: 30 days US/Canada/Japan-FIH, 45+5 days EU with 12-day RFIs, 60 days China, about 5-day CTN notification versus a 50-day CTA target in Australia [PMID:40303377; PMID:37389794; PMID:37125239].
In Australia, choose CTN versus CTA early. CTA is mandatory for high-risk biologicals and involves TGA safety evaluation [PMID:40303377].
The US phase 1 CGMP exemption (2008 rule) is US-specific. Do not assume equivalent relief for EU, Japanese or Chinese clinical supply [PMID:18850678].

Post-approval divergence is large: global change approvals can take 3–5 years, and Q12 uptake is uneven (US/Japan implemented, China pilot, EU legislation under revision as of 2024). Generate enhanced development data during phase 2-3 so ECs/PACMPs can be proposed at filing [PMID:39179719; PMID:40839206].

NOT verified this session (low confidence): Health Canada CTA quality summary template requirements; Japanese GMP-for-investigational-products notification; EMA IMP quality guideline identifiers and phase-specific text; China CDE phase-specific pharmaceutical guidance; any current Chinese IND review pilot shorter than 60 days.
commonDeficiencies: See the region-specific deficiency notes. Recurring cross-region themes are unjustified specifications, thin stability data, and inadequate potency or comparability bridging [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3; PMID:37886603; PMID:37125239].

notes.topic: How should release specifications for a clinical-stage biologic be set and tightened from phase 1 to licensure?
notes.summary: Specifications for biological investigational products are expected to evolve. Early limits are practical operational limits based on preclinical, toxicology and early clinical lots. They are refined as assay validation, manufacturing experience and characterisation accumulate, and become registered specifications at licensure. Industry guidance places this in a control strategy under ICH Q8(R2)/Q11/Q9/Q10, with revisions managed in a flexible quality system. Regulators and industry are discussing patient-centric, globally harmonised specifications in parallel with the ICH Q6(R1) revision; its status was not verified here. EU assessors most frequently object to specifications that are inadequately justified or incomplete, so each limit should be traced to batch data, clinical exposure and method capability.
keyPoints: FDA (CBER) describes specification setting as phased: realistic or practical operational limits first, then more stringent specifications as data from preclinical, toxicology and clinical lots and assay validation accumulate [PMID:9413677].
After approval, accumulated test results continue to refine specifications [PMID:9413677].

An industry best-practice paper places clinical biological specifications within Q8(R2)/Q11 development, Q9 QRM and Q10 quality systems. It gives a case study of managing IMP specification revisions in a flexible quality system [PMID:26429107].

A 2025 IABS workshop covered updates on ICH Q6(R1) revisions, enhanced versus traditional specification setting, separating specifications from process monitoring, and 'one product-one specification' via reliance [PMID:42790270].
Inadequately justified or incomplete specifications were the most prominent IMPD deficiency in EU CTAs from 2015 to 2024 [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
Q6(R1) status (draft or Step reached) as of 2026-10 was NOT verified in this research.
commonDeficiencies: Inadequately justified or incomplete specifications (EU IMPD) [DOI:10.1007/s43441-026-01046-3].
Release specifications listed among typical FDA CMC hold triggers for CGT INDs [PMID:37886603].
Unnecessary specifications on non-critical quality attributes were highlighted for biotherapeutics [PMID:42790270].

notes.topic: What viral safety package does a cell-line-derived biologic need for a first-in-human IND or IMPD under ICH Q5A(R2)?
notes.summary: ICH Q5A(R2) governs the viral safety of biotechnology products made from human or animal cell lines. ICH adopted it at Step 4 on 1 November 2023, and FDA issued it as final guidance in January 2024, replacing the 1998 Q5A. It rests on three complementary approaches: (1) select and test the cell lines and raw materials; (2) test the product at suitable production steps, namely the cell banks, cells at the limit of in vitro cell age and the unprocessed bulk; and (3) show how much virus the purification process clears. R2 adds next-generation sequencing (NGS) for broad virus detection, use of platform or prior-knowledge clearance data and continuous-manufacturing considerations. It also extends scope to some viral-vector products that can undergo viral clearance. Q5A(R2) defines the marketing data set, but how much is needed for a first clinical trial is set by each region: the EU biological IMP guideline expects viral safety to be addressed from the first trial, and FDA's 2026 first-in-human (FIH) clarification for CDER recombinant products reportedly lists a product-specific viral clearance study as generally not needed at FIH; that wording should be checked before use. The evaluation goes in 3.2.A.2, cross-referenced to 3.2.S.2.3 (cell banks and raw materials) and 3.2.S.2.2 (process).
keyPoints: Test the Master Cell Bank (MCB), the Working Cell Bank (WCB) as applicable, and cells at the limit of in vitro cell age for adventitious and endogenous viruses, and test each unprocessed bulk harvest. Summarize the results in 3.2.A.2. [ICH Q5A(R2); ICH Q5D]

Show viral clearance with scaled-down models of purification steps spiked with relevant and model viruses, and report log10 reduction factors per step. For rodent cell lines, clearance of endogenous retrovirus-like particles must be addressed. [ICH Q5A(R2); PMID:41678029]

Q5A(R2) lets non-targeted NGS replace in vivo adventitious-virus assays and virus-specific PCR (e.g., antibody-production tests) without a head-to-head comparison, and supplement or replace cell-culture infectivity assays, provided the validation package is suitable. [PMID:40945333]

For NGS in regulatory submissions, CBER generally expects the WHO International Reference Panel for NGS adventitious-virus detection, or an equivalent characterized material, to be used in validation. [PMID:40945333]
A secondary source reports that Q5A(R2) calls a clearance step effective at ≥4 log10 reduction. Check this against the guideline text before quoting it as a requirement. [PMID:39906555]
EU: address viral safety from the first trial in the IMPD, covering raw-material control, cell bank testing and process clearance capacity. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2]

US FIH (CDER recombinant products): FDA's June 2026 clarification lists a product-specific viral clearance study as generally not needed at FIH. Read the accompanying risk-assessment expectations in the PDF before relying on this. [FDA media/193164]

Assess and document viral and TSE risk for animal-derived raw materials. Industry-wide contamination data from the Consortium on Adventitious Agent Contamination in Biomanufacturing (CAACB) cover the contaminants, their sources and the cell lines affected, and are the evidence base for raw-material controls. [PMID:32341561]
NGS has been shown to detect viruses in cell substrates and bulk harvest with sensitivity similar to PCR and without prior knowledge of the virus. [PMID:30030351]
commonDeficiencies: The scaled-down viral clearance model is not shown to represent the manufacturing step. For example, impurities in the virus spike can depress virus-filter performance in the small-scale study. [PMID:26048749]

Unexpected positive results in MCB adventitious-agent testing are not root-caused. In one published case, the contaminant came from the testing laboratory's screening system rather than the MCB. [PMID:21502054; PMID:18757212]
Viral contamination of production cultures does occur despite controls, and recovery is costly. [PMID:32341561]

notes.topic: What replication-competent virus and adventitious-agent testing does a viral-vector gene therapy IND need, including RCR/RCL testing for retroviral and lentiviral vectors?
notes.summary: FDA's January 2020 gene therapy CMC guidance puts two things in 3.2.A.2: risk assessments for human- or animal-derived materials (viral clearance or inactivation, or adventitious-agent testing of source material, with representative certificates of analysis) and evidence that replication-incompetent vectors are free of replication-competent virus. For gammaretroviral and lentiviral vectors, FDA's companion January 2020 guidance on testing for replication-competent retrovirus (RCR) sets the testing points: vector material, end-of-production cells, ex vivo transduced cells, and patient monitoring after treatment. A 2025 review summarizes that guidance as recommending testing of 1% or 1×10^8 end-of-production cells, whichever is less. The same review says it replaced the earlier '5% of crude supernatant or 300 mL' vector test with testing an amount equal to three patient doses, and that EMA no longer requires testing of ex vivo transduced cells when vector testing gives enough confidence under a risk assessment. Culture-based replication-competent lentivirus (RCL) assays can take up to about 6 weeks, so programs infusing fresh cells have qualified rapid qPCR assays (e.g., for VSV-G). National Gene Vector Biorepository data found no RCR in 1,595 post-treatment samples from 60 trials.
keyPoints: Put adventitious-agent risk assessments for biological materials, with representative certificates of analysis, and evidence of absence of replication-competent virus in 3.2.A.2. [FDA GT CMC guidance 2020]
Test 1% or 1×10^8 end-of-production cells per batch, whichever is less, as summarized from FDA's 2020 RCR guidance. [PMID:41141960]
Test vector material equal to three patient doses; FDA's 2020 RCR guidance introduced this in place of the earlier '5% of crude supernatant or 300 mL' approach. [PMID:41141960]
US: test ex vivo transduced cell products for RCR/RCL regardless of ex vivo expansion time, unless reduced or no testing is justified with data in the IND. [PMID:41141960]
EU: testing of ex vivo transduced cells may be omitted when RCV testing of the vector material provides the necessary confidence under a risk assessment. [PMID:41141960]
Keep FDA's RCR patient-monitoring plan in the protocol. Cumulative surveillance found no RCR in 338 pre-treatment and 1,595 post-treatment samples from 737 patients in 60 trials. [PMID:36518078]
For fresh (non-cryopreserved) cell products, a qualified qPCR RCL assay can support release, since cell-based RCL assays can take up to about 6 weeks. [PMID:29034262]
Vectors with non-standard envelopes may need a purpose-built RCL assay format. Its evaluation criteria and positive controls can be agreed with FDA. [PMID:26029728]
Characterize derivative packaging or producer cell lines made with component-delivery retroviral vectors for RCV as well as for endogenous retrovirus. [PMID:41141960]
commonDeficiencies: The RCL assay is not shown to amplify a hypothetical RCL arising from the specific vector system, which is a particular issue for non-standard pseudotypes. [PMID:26029728]
Sponsors interpret RCV testing amounts and testing points inconsistently. [PMID:41141960]
Two of five publicly announced lentiviral-vector clinical holds in 2020–2022 were CMC-triggered; the specific issues were not disclosed. [PMID:37886603]

notes.topic: What cell bank, expression-construct and clonality characterization must be in place before first-in-human for a recombinant biologic or a vector-producing cell line (ICH Q5D, Q5B)?
notes.summary: ICH Q5D (Step 4, 16 July 1997) requires documentation of three things: where the cell substrate came from and its history, how the production cell line was generated, and a Master/Working Cell Bank system. The banks must be characterized for identity, purity (microbial, mycoplasma, adventitious and endogenous viruses, cross-contamination) and stability through the proposed in vitro cell age. ICH Q5B (30 November 1995) requires the expression construct to be characterized and the coding sequence and genetic stability confirmed in production cells, including at the limit of in vitro cell age. Regulators now expect robust evidence that the production cell line came from a single cell. Where clonality assurance has been weak, sponsors have faced augmented control strategies, and legacy lines have been supported by analytical subcloning of the MCB. The same principles apply to allogeneic cell banks for cell therapy and to producer or packaging cell lines for viral vectors. This information belongs in 3.2.S.2.3, with viral testing summarized in 3.2.A.2.
keyPoints: Before FIH, characterize an MCB for identity, sterility, mycoplasma and adventitious/endogenous viruses. Test the WCB to a reduced extent and test cells at the limit of in vitro cell age once. [ICH Q5D; ICH Q5A(R2)]
Document the history of the cell line, including any exposure to animal-derived reagents during development. [ICH Q5D]
Describe the expression construct and confirm the coding sequence and genetic stability up to the limit of in vitro cell age used for production. [ICH Q5B]

Give quantitative clonality evidence, such as imaged single-cell deposition with whole-well imaging and a calculated probability of clonality. Two rounds of limiting dilution was the historical standard. [PMID:40034018; PMID:31841273]

If clonality assurance for a legacy line is weak, expect requests for augmented control strategies. Analytical subcloning of the MCB, for example showing a conserved integration junction across 24 subclones, has been used retrospectively. [PMID:34586757]
Qualify allogeneic cell sources for cell therapies to an extent similar to biologics MCB/WCB, with defined donor selection criteria. [PMID:35646952]
commonDeficiencies: Insufficient assurance that the production cell line is clonal. [PMID:34586757]
Unexplained adventitious-agent signals during MCB testing without a documented root-cause investigation. [PMID:21502054; PMID:18757212]
Variability between allogeneic donors is not addressed by donor criteria and characterization. [PMID:35646952]

notes.topic: How should drug substance and drug product specifications for a phase 1 biologic be set and justified (ICH Q6B, phase-appropriate)?
notes.summary: ICH Q6B (Step 4 on 10 March 1999; FDA guidance August 1999) defines a specification for a biotechnological product as identity, purity and impurities, potency (biological activity) and quantity, plus general tests. Acceptance criteria are justified from preclinical and clinical lots, consistency lots, stability data and development data. Q6B is written for marketing applications and is due to be replaced by Q6(R1), with Step 2 targeted for November 2026 and Step 4 for June 2027. In a survey of 19 companies, most sponsors set FIH specifications from platform knowledge, justified early acceptance criteria from limited molecule-specific data, and used non-numerical criteria for some attributes. For CDER recombinant products, FDA's June 2026 FIH clarification says analytical method validation data are not expected in an original FIH IND, and a potency assay is not expected for simple proteins shown to lack higher-order structure. FDA's May 2026 CGT flexibilities guidance allows permissive early release criteria where safety is not compromised but expects acceptance criteria to be defined before phase 2/3.
keyPoints: Cover identity, purity and impurities, potency, quantity and general (compendial) tests in drug substance and drug product specifications. [ICH Q6B]
Justify FIH acceptance criteria from lots used in toxicology studies, early process data and platform experience when molecule-specific data are limited. [PMID:30528942; ICH Q6B]

Non-numerical acceptance criteria are a recognized early-phase option for some characterization attributes. Hold safety attributes such as sterility and endotoxin to defined limits from the first clinical lot; this is a general expectation, not a quoted rule. [PMID:30528942]

US FIH (CDER recombinant products): method validation data are not expected. A potency assay is not expected for simple proteins without higher-order structure, and potency characterization results may suffice if QC method development is incomplete. [FDA media/193164]
US CGT: permissive early release criteria are acceptable if safety is not compromised, but acceptance criteria must be defined before phase 2/3. [FDA guidance May 2026, media/192321]
Q6A and Q6B apply until Q6(R1) reaches Step 4. Q6(R1) will merge them and extend specification principles to cell and gene therapies. [ICH Q6(R1) concept paper 2024]
commonDeficiencies: Specifications and their justification were the most frequent US BLA quality issue (18%) for approved cell-gene therapies. FDA requested changes to commercial lot release specifications, and EMA recommended re-evaluating acceptance criteria with post-approval data. [PMID:41678030]
Release specifications are on FDA's list of typical CMC deficiencies that lead to cell and gene therapy clinical holds. [PMID:37886603]

notes.topic: How should product-related impurities, aggregates and subvisible particles be characterized and controlled for a clinical-stage protein therapeutic?
notes.summary: ICH Q6B separates product-related substances (variants with activity comparable to the desired product) from product-related impurities such as aggregates, fragments and degradation products, which must be characterized and controlled. Q6B also states that pharmacopoeial particulate-matter requirements apply to biotechnological products. Aggregates are an established immunogenicity risk factor: large, highly arrayed aggregates of native-like protein can strongly drive antibody responses, and changes to manufacturing or packaging can shift aggregate profiles. USP <788> limits particles ≥10 µm to ≤6000 and ≥25 µm to ≤600 per container but does not monitor the 0.1–10 µm range, so orthogonal methods are recommended for characterization. An AAPS survey found that compendial particle methods plus SEC are the main early-phase controls, with extended characterization added later and only robust, stability-indicating methods used for GMP release. For AAV vectors, empty and partial capsids are the equivalent product-related impurity class.
keyPoints: Characterize size variants (SEC for soluble aggregates and fragments) and other product-related variants, and set acceptance criteria in drug substance and drug product release and stability specifications. [ICH Q6B; PMID:31677011]
Meet compendial subvisible particle limits at release. USP <788> light obscuration allows ≤6000 particles ≥10 µm and ≤600 particles ≥25 µm per container. [USP <788>; PMID:18704929]
During development, characterize particles below 10 µm with orthogonal techniques such as flow imaging, because compendial tests do not count them. [PMID:18704929; PMID:19519412]

Re-examine aggregate and particle profiles after changes to process, formulation, container closure or filling equipment. In one development program, prefilled syringes had higher subvisible particles than vials. [PMID:20888784; PMID:17025268]
Feed aggregate and particle data into the immunogenicity risk assessment. [PMID:17025268]
For AAV, quantify empty, partial and full capsids with orthogonal methods (AUC, cryo-TEM, CDMS, AEX, SEC-MALS, or genome-to-capsid ratio by qPCR/ddPCR with ELISA). [PMID:39234444]
commonDeficiencies: Particles below 10 µm are not characterized; a product can meet USP <788> while containing very large numbers of 1–10 µm protein particles. [PMID:18704929]
Peginesatide lots linked to severe adverse reactions, including 7 deaths, had particle populations that flow-imaging morphology could distinguish from those of unaffected lots. [PMID:29409840]
Changing the presentation, for example from vial to prefilled syringe, raised subvisible particle levels in a development comparability study. [PMID:20888784]

notes.topic: What potency assay is expected for a cell or gene therapy at each clinical phase, and when must it be validated?
notes.summary: FDA's final guidance 'Potency Tests for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products' (January 2011) expects potency information at every IND phase. It wants suitable potency assays in place before studies meant to provide primary evidence of effectiveness, and validated lot-release potency assays for a BLA. The December 2023 draft 'Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products', intended to replace it, treats potency as a risk-based strategy spanning process design, material and in-process controls, and release assays; it was not confirmed final as of 2026-10-04. Assay development and validation follow ICH Q14 and Q2(R2), both adopted on 1 November 2023 and issued by FDA in March 2024. For the 31 FDA-approved cell therapy products, an estimated 104 potency tests were used (about 3.4 per product); of the 71 non-redacted tests, 52% measured viability or count and 27% measured expression. Approved CAR-T products are released with an IFN-γ secretion assay as the accepted surrogate potency method, and potency-assay issues were the most frequent EU major objection (25%) in marketing applications for cell-gene therapies.
keyPoints: Provide potency data at every phase. A qualified rather than fully validated assay is acceptable early; FDA's CAR-T draft guidance does not require fully validated potency assays for early-phase lot release. [FDA potency guidance 2011; PMID:40442256]

Have suitable, preferably mechanism-linked potency assays in place before pivotal studies, so that potency can be correlated with clinical outcome and used for comparability. [FDA potency guidance 2011; PMID:35646952]
Validate lot-release potency assays for the BLA/MAA following ICH Q2(R2) and Q14. [FDA potency guidance 2011; ICH Q2(R2); ICH Q14]
Where no single assay captures the mechanism of action, use a matrix of assays, e.g., infectivity or transduction plus a cell-based measure of transgene function for vectors. [PMID:35646952]
Surrogate release assays are accepted by FDA and EU authorities when correlated during development with a functional assay. [PMID:35646952]
For AAV, keep titer assays (vector genomes, capsids, infectivity) separate from potency assays that measure transgene expression and function. [PMID:39234444]
CAR-T: release on IFN-γ secretion after antigen-specific stimulation, with antigen-negative controls to show the response is CAR-specific. [PMID:40442256; PMID:41678030]

EU: include a biological activity or potency assay in release specifications for biological IMPs, with validation maturing toward confirmatory trials. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2; EMA/CAT/22473/2025]
commonDeficiencies: Potency-assay issues were the most frequent EU major objection (25%) for approved cell-gene therapies. In one review, a tumor-killing release assay was replaced by an IFN-γ assay with a commitment to re-evaluate the limits. [PMID:41678030]
FDA lists the lack of an adequate potency assay among typical CMC clinical-hold deficiencies. One CGT partial hold required an improved potency assay before it was lifted. [PMID:37886603]
Programs rely heavily on viability, count and expression measurements; true bioassays were reported for only 7 of 31 approved cell therapy products. [PMID:40038737]
Potency testing is a frequent subject of post-marketing commitments. [PMID:41678030]

notes.topic: When a biologic's manufacturing process changes between toxicology, phase 1 and pivotal lots, what comparability data are expected (ICH Q5E)?
notes.summary: ICH Q5E (Step 4 on 18 November 2004; FDA guidance June 2005) sets the principles for comparing product made before and after a process change, during development or after approval. The exercise is led by quality data: it must show the pre- and post-change products are highly similar and that any differences in quality attributes do not adversely affect safety or efficacy. Nonclinical or clinical bridging is added when analytical data are not enough. During development the depth of the exercise scales with stage and risk. Batch comparability data typically combine in-process controls, release results, extended characterization and stability (including forced degradation) for pre- and post-change lots. Published monoclonal antibody (mAb) case studies show that a cell line or process change can shift sialylation and C-terminal lysine, while scale-up and site transfer often have no effect. An antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) program bridged its early- and late-phase processes under Q5E using release, physicochemical, biophysical, biological and forced-degradation data. Major changes are best made before pivotal studies, because clinical bridging may not be feasible afterwards.
keyPoints: Run a risk-based comparability exercise for process changes between nonclinical, early clinical and later material. Describe the change history and comparability results in 3.2.S.2.6 and 3.2.P.2.3. [ICH Q5E; EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2]
Compare retained pre-change lots and post-change lots side by side, using release tests, extended characterization, stability and forced degradation. [PMID:37428761; PMID:23146362; PMID:35646952]

Pre-specify acceptance criteria that reflect process and analytical variability. EU assessors prefer side-by-side results with standard deviations; FDA may ask you to justify the statistical approach. [PMID:35646952]
After a cell line or upstream change, expect and evaluate glycan and charge-variant shifts (e.g., sialylation, C-terminal lysine) for functional impact. [PMID:20888784]
Show that material used in toxicology studies represents the clinical material. [PMID:37886603]
Finish major process changes before pivotal studies. [PMID:35646952]
commonDeficiencies: Failure to show that nonclinical material represents clinical material is a recognized trigger for clinical holds. [PMID:37886603]
FDA lists comparability bridging studies and substantive manufacturing changes among typical CMC clinical-hold deficiencies. [PMID:37886603]
Too few retained samples of earlier batches to support later comparability, particularly for small-batch cell-based products. [PMID:35646952]

notes.topic: How should comparability be shown for manufacturing changes to a cell or gene therapy during clinical development?
notes.summary: FDA's July 2023 draft guidance 'Manufacturing Changes and Comparability for Human Cellular and Gene Therapy Products' was not confirmed final as of 2026-10-04. It asks sponsors to risk-assess every manufacturing change, scale the comparability study to that risk, and choose suitable statistical designs such as split-apheresis studies for autologous products. FDA's May 2026 CMC flexibilities guidance allows limited comparability data for minor, low-risk changes, submitted before post-change product is given to patients. ICH Q5E principles apply. An ICH Q5E annex for ATMPs such as CAR-T and AAV is reportedly in development, but no draft was confirmed. Among approved cell-gene therapies, comparability was the second most frequent EU major objection (19%) and a frequent 'other concern' (17%); some residual differences were handled through post-approval commitments. Small lot numbers and donor variability make statistical comparability hard: with 3–5 donors, a paired split-apheresis analysis can be underpowered for some quality attributes.
keyPoints: Risk-assess every CGT manufacturing change and size the comparability study to that risk. [FDA draft guidance July 2023; FDA guidance May 2026]
For minor, low-risk changes, limited comparability data may suffice, but they must be submitted before any patient receives post-change product. [FDA guidance May 2026, media/192321]
For autologous products, consider split-apheresis designs, and power them prospectively; 3–5 donors may be too few for a paired analysis of some attributes. [PMID:39285085]
Keep a tabulated manufacturing history covering vector, active substance and finished product, with the rationale for each change. [PMID:41678030]
Base comparability on analytical studies beyond release specifications. Add nonclinical data, and clinical data as a last resort, if analytics are insufficient. [PMID:41678030]
Support raw-material changes with a documented comparability study, for example replacing a material with a GMP-compliant grade. [PMID:36894437]
commonDeficiencies: Process comparability accounted for 19% of EU major objections and 17% of 'other concerns' for approved cell-gene therapies. [PMID:41678030]
Regulators issued repeated information requests on comparability across approved advanced therapies. [PMID:34278825]
FDA counts comparability bridging and substantive manufacturing changes among typical CGT clinical-hold deficiencies. [PMID:37886603]

notes.topic: What must the CMC section of a human gene therapy IND contain under FDA's January 2020 guidance?
notes.summary: FDA's final guidance 'Chemistry, Manufacturing, and Control (CMC) Information for Human Gene Therapy INDs' (January 2020) replaced the April 2008 reviewer guidance. It organizes gene therapy IND CMC content by CTD Module 3, including 3.2.A.1 (facilities and equipment) and 3.2.A.2 (adventitious agents safety evaluation). Not every section must be complete in the original IND, a Module 2.3 quality overall summary (QOS) is recommended, and process validation is not required for early-stage manufacturing. Sponsors describe and qualify starting materials such as plasmids, cell banks and virus banks, describe the manufacturing process and controls, and give drug substance and drug product specifications for safety, identity, purity, strength and potency, plus stability data supporting clinical use. Absence of replication-competent virus is a product-specific safety test. FDA's May 2026 CGT CMC flexibilities guidance adds permissive early release criteria, risk-based comparability and a scientifically justified number of PPQ batches, while keeping full statutory compliance. In 2020–2022, CMC triggered 7 of 33 publicly announced CGT clinical holds, and AAV programs accounted for 15 of the 33.
keyPoints: Organize CMC under Module 3, including 3.2.A.1 and 3.2.A.2. Partially complete sections are acceptable in the original IND, and a 2.3 QOS is recommended. [FDA GT CMC guidance 2020]

Process validation is not required for early-stage manufacturing. Manufacture phase 1 material under phase-appropriate CGMP. [FDA GT CMC guidance 2020; FDA CGMP for Phase 1 Investigational Drugs 2008]
Qualify plasmids, cell banks, virus banks and biological reagents, and give adventitious-agent risk assessments in 3.2.A.2. [FDA GT CMC guidance 2020]
AAV specifications should cover genome titer (qPCR/ddPCR), capsid titer, empty/full ratio, identity, purity, potency and, increasingly, genome integrity. [PMID:39234444]
Provide data on compatibility with administration devices and containers, and on stability during transport. [PMID:37886603]

Use INTERACT and pre-IND meetings for CMC questions. FDA gave advice on process development, GMP manufacturing, quality attributes, potency assay and device compatibility, but limited CMC information produced only general advice. [PMID:39976996]
Under CBER's May 2026 flexibilities, define release acceptance criteria before phase 2/3 and justify the number of PPQ batches scientifically. [FDA guidance May 2026, media/192321]
commonDeficiencies: FDA-cited typical CGT clinical-hold CMC deficiencies: compatibility with administration devices and containers, stability during transport, adequate potency assays, comparability bridging studies, substantive manufacturing changes and release specifications. [PMID:37886603]

Incomplete CMC information in an early-meeting package yields only general rather than product-specific FDA advice. [PMID:39976996]

notes.topic: How should residual host-cell and plasmid DNA and empty or partial capsids be controlled and justified for an AAV gene therapy in clinical development?
notes.summary: FDA guidance for human gene therapy products recommends limiting residual host-cell DNA to less than 10 ng per dose with fragments below about 200 bp. These thresholds come from 1998 WHO recommendations for biologics made in cell substrates, and recent data show many rAAV products exceed them (reported range 1–210 pg per 1×10^9 genome copies). Total DNA impurities, from plasmid, helper and host-cell sequences, have been reported at 0.5–13% of vector genomes depending on method and process, and the amount of host-cell DNA measured depends on the qPCR target (18S versus Alu gave about 95 versus 15 ng per 1×10^12 vector genomes in one study). Long-read sequencing showed packaged impurities were mostly fragmented: no complete human open reading frames were found, and plasmid-derived transcripts in dosed mice were below 0.01% of transgene transcripts. Such data support a data-based risk assessment where the default limits cannot be met. Empty and partial capsids are product-related impurities that can affect potency and immunogenicity, so their ratio should be measured by orthogonal methods and controlled.
keyPoints: Quantify residual host-cell DNA (amount and size distribution) and residual plasmid sequences (e.g., Rep/Cap, antibiotic-resistance gene, adenoviral helper genes) on each drug substance or drug product lot. [PMID:40599703; FDA GT CMC guidance 2020]

Measure against the <10 ng/dose and <200 bp recommendations. If they are exceeded, justify with a risk assessment that can include long-read sequencing of packaged impurities for complete open reading frames and transcription potential. [PMID:40599703]
State the residual-DNA assay target and its standard, since results differ several-fold between targets such as 18S and Alu. [PMID:40599703]
Quantify empty, partial and full capsids with orthogonal methods and set an acceptance criterion or report-and-trend strategy appropriate to the phase. [PMID:39234444]
Consider the immunogenicity and dose-definition impact of empty capsids when setting strength and potency criteria. [PMID:35646952]

Reduce impurities through vector and process design, e.g., nuclease treatment, affinity plus anion-exchange purification and promoter redesign to limit Rep/Cap expression, especially for doses above 1×10^14 GC/kg. [PMID:40599703]
commonDeficiencies: Residual DNA reported only as mass without size distribution or sequence identity, so oncogenic or expression risk cannot be assessed. [PMID:40599703]
Empty/full ratio measured by a single method with uncharacterized variability, with no reference material. [PMID:39234444]
Empty capsids, which are common with multi-plasmid processes, are not addressed in the immunogenicity and dose rationale. [PMID:35646952]

notes.topic: What release testing and CMC content are expected for a somatic cell therapy (including CAR-T) IND or CTA?
notes.summary: FDA's April 2008 guidance 'Content and Review of CMC Information for Human Somatic Cell Therapy INDs' sets out the CMC content of a cell therapy IND: components and reagents, source material, manufacturing procedures, release testing, stability and container closure. FDA still lists it, but its currency in 2026 was not independently confirmed. Standards for sterility, purity, potency and mycoplasma for licensed biologics are in 21 CFR Part 610, and donor eligibility for human cells is in 21 CFR Part 1271. Typical release tests are sterility, mycoplasma, endotoxin, identity, purity, dose or viability and potency, plus vector copy number and RCR/RCL for genetically modified cells; a viability criterion of ≥70% is commonly applied. The compendial mycoplasma culture (Ph. Eur. 2.6.7 / USP <63>) takes 28 days and about 15 mL, so validated nucleic-acid amplification tests are accepted for short-shelf-life products. Endotoxin limits derive from the 5 EU/kg/h threshold and the method must be validated against matrix interference. For autologous products made in one continuous process, specifications may be set only for the finished product. Biological raw and ancillary materials need qualification (Ph. Eur. 5.2.12, USP <1043>); US INDs can reference Drug Master Files (DMFs) for ancillary materials, whereas EU CTAs must disclose raw-material data.
keyPoints: Release every lot for sterility, mycoplasma, endotoxin, identity, purity, dose and viability, and potency, with acceptance criteria. [FDA SCT CMC guidance 2008; 21 CFR 610; PMID:42427427]

If the compendial 28-day culture cannot fit the shelf life, use a validated rapid mycoplasma NAT; re-verify detection limits and matrix on site even for commercial kits. [Ph. Eur. 2.6.7; PMID:40442256]
Convert endotoxin results to EU/kg of the patient dose against the 5 EU/kg/h threshold, and validate the LAL or recombinant factor C method for matrix interference. [PMID:40442256]
For genetically modified cells, measure vector copy number with a validated qPCR or ddPCR method and test for RCR/RCL. [PMID:40442256; FDA RCR guidance 2020]
Release CAR-T for potency with an antigen-specific IFN-γ assay, as used for all approved CAR-T products, and support it with CAR expression and viability. [PMID:40442256; PMID:41678030]

A viability acceptance criterion of ≥70% is common practice. FDA's 2008 SCT guidance is believed to recommend 70% or a data-supported lower limit, but that guidance text was not verified this session. [PMID:42427427]
Qualify biological raw materials per Ph. Eur. 5.2.12 or USP <1043>, and agree any use of research-grade materials with regulators before toxicology and first clinical lots. [PMID:35646952]
For continuous autologous processes, finished-product specifications, analytical procedures and batch analysis without a separate active-substance specification have been accepted. [PMID:41678030]
For allogeneic cells, establish donor eligibility (screening and testing) under 21 CFR Part 1271. [21 CFR 1271; PMID:37886603]
commonDeficiencies: FDA requested clearer validation of mycoplasma tests and post-marketing commitments on sterility-assay validation for approved cell-gene therapies. [PMID:41678030]
Container-closure integrity and extractables/leachables assessments were insufficient. [PMID:41678030]
Agencies did not consider healthy-donor surrogate starting material fully representative of patient material for process qualification. [PMID:41678030]
Out-of-specification results for critical attributes (e.g., final CAR-positive cell number) in autologous manufacturing left some patients untreated. [PMID:35646952]
Donor-eligibility and CMC deficiencies led to a cell therapy clinical hold, lifted after CMC amendments about 6 months later. [PMID:37886603]

notes.topic: What does the EU guideline on investigational ATMPs (EMA/CAT/22473/2025) require for the quality part of an ATMP clinical trial application?
notes.summary: EMA/CAT/22473/2025, 'Guideline on quality, non-clinical and clinical requirements for investigational advanced therapy medicinal products in clinical trials', was adopted by CAT on 6 December 2024 and by CHMP on 20 January 2025, and has applied since 1 July 2025. It finalizes drafts first consulted on in 2019. It covers gene therapy, somatic cell therapy, tissue-engineered and combined ATMPs in exploratory and confirmatory trials, and consolidates content from more than 40 guidelines and reflection papers. The guideline is multidisciplinary and risk-based: the extent of quality, non-clinical and clinical data may be adapted to identified risks and the stage of development. ATMP clinical trial applications go through Regulation (EU) No 536/2014, and gene therapy products, including genetically modified cells, additionally need GMO (environmental risk) approval before clinical use. Unlike the US, the EU has no Drug Master File route for raw materials, so raw-material data must be in the application. Manufacture falls under EU GMP for ATMPs (EudraLex Volume 4, Part IV); the Part IV identifiers and dates were not verified this session.
keyPoints: Since 1 July 2025, prepare the quality, non-clinical and clinical parts of investigational ATMP CTAs under EMA/CAT/22473/2025. [EMA/CAT/22473/2025]
Scale quality data to identified risks and the development stage, and justify reduced data with a documented risk-based approach. [EMA/CAT/22473/2025; PMID:37526839]
Plan the national GMO application for gene therapy products and genetically modified cells in parallel with the CTA, as it can delay first-in-human. [PMID:35646952]
Put raw-material qualification data directly in the CTA, because the EU has no DMF-type referencing for ancillary materials. [PMID:35646952]
Manufacture investigational ATMPs to EU GMP for ATMPs (EudraLex Volume 4, Part IV). [EudraLex Volume 4]

Use national innovation offices, EMA's Innovation Task Force or national scientific advice before FIH. Since 2022 under the CTR, a single CTA via CTIS is assessed by all concerned member states. [PMID:35646952; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014]
Expect EU assessors to focus on potency assays and process comparability, the top EU major-objection areas at marketing authorization. [PMID:41678030]
commonDeficiencies: Parallel GMO procedures in the EU delay the start of first-in-human studies. [PMID:35646952]

In MAAs for cell-gene therapies, 6 of 7 accelerated assessments were reverted to standard timelines, citing GMP inspection and certification issues, major objections, and incomplete data sets. [PMID:41678030]
Potency-assay and comparability major objections. [PMID:41678030]

notes.topic: What does the EU require in the IMPD quality section for a biological (non-ATMP) investigational product?
notes.summary: For biological IMPs without a simplified IMPD, the quality part of the IMPD follows EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2. CHMP adopted it on 27 January 2022, it took effect on 31 January 2022, it supersedes Rev. 1, and it was prepared to implement Regulation (EU) No 536/2014. The IMPD is structured on CTD Module 3 and must contain the most up-to-date information relevant to the trial at submission. As captured in the existing corpus at low confidence, the guideline expects four things: viral safety addressed from the first trial (raw-material control, cell bank testing, clearance capacity); a biological activity or potency assay in release specifications, with validation maturing toward confirmatory trials; risk-based comparability whenever the process changes, especially relative to batches used in nonclinical and earlier clinical studies; and phase-appropriate specifications. Section-level wording was not verified this session. MHRA assessors have described CTA quality review as centred on whether risks to trial subjects have been identified and mitigated.
keyPoints: Prepare the biological IMPD quality section under EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2, structured on CTD Module 3. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2; Regulation (EU) No 536/2014]
Address adventitious-agent and viral safety from the first clinical trial. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2]
Include a potency or biological activity assay in release specifications, with phase-appropriate validation. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2]
Support process changes with risk-based comparability between pre- and post-change material, particularly against nonclinical and earlier clinical batches. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2; ICH Q5E]
Phase-appropriate specification practice, such as platform-justified FIH criteria and selective non-numerical criteria for characterization attributes, is widely used by industry. [PMID:30528942]
Frame the IMPD around identified risks to trial subjects and how they are mitigated, which is the lens CTA quality assessors use. [PMID:23216470]
commonDeficiencies: Quality data do not show that risks to trial subjects have been identified and mitigated. [PMID:23216470]
Comparability gaps between nonclinical, early clinical and current material. [EMA/CHMP/BWP/534898/2008 Rev. 2; PMID:35646952]
