notes.topic: How is the acceptable intake for a nitrosamine impurity, including an NDSRI, established, and how do FDA and EMA approaches differ?
notes.summary: N-nitrosamines are a cohort of concern under ICH M7, so the 1.5 µg/day TTC does not apply by default. The first choice is a compound-specific AI from robust carcinogenicity data (for example NDMA 96 ng/day and NDEA 26.5 ng/day), then read-across from a suitable surrogate. Where neither is available, as for most nitrosamine drug substance-related impurities (NDSRIs), the Carcinogenic Potency Categorization Approach (CPCA) assigns one of five potency categories. It scores α-hydrogen counts and activating/deactivating structural features, and each category carries a predefined AI. FDA issued a final guidance in August 2023 recommending CPCA-based AIs for NDSRIs; Health Canada and EMA adopted the approach, and Japan's MHLW is reported to accept it. Predefined AIs range from 18 ng/day (EMA) or 26.5 ng/day (FDA) for Category 1 up to 1500 ng/day. The agencies differ on Ames data: EMA may permit 1.5 µg/day for a nitrosamine negative in an Enhanced Ames Test (EAT), whereas FDA may not accept a negative Ames alone and may request in vitro mammalian mutation and metabolism data.
keyPoints: CPCA categories: Category 1 = 26.5 ng/day (FDA) / 18 ng/day (EMA); Category 2 = 100 ng/day (confirmed: N-nitroso reboxetine and NMOR example). Category 3 = 400 ng/day and Categories 4–5 = 1500 ng/day are from the guidance as known to the author (range 18/26.5–1500 confirmed in literature).

EAT conditions described in the literature: 30-minute pre-incubation, specified base-substitution strains (TA1535, TA100, WP2 uvrA (pKM101)), restricted solvent type and volume, 30% rat and hamster liver S9, and two nitrosamine-specific positive controls (Zhang et al. 2025). Recent FDA guidance is reported to accept water, methanol or DMSO (minimal volume) as solvents and to recommend supporting metabolism data (Thomas et al. 2025).

Regulators no longer accept a negative standard or enhanced Ames alone as sufficient to classify a nitrosamine as M7 Class 5 without further support; extensive follow-up such as transgenic rodent assays may be required (Thomas et al. 2025).

Data-driven AIs above the CPCA value are possible. Example: BMD analysis of in vivo Duplex Sequencing data supported 24,000 ng/day for N-nitroso reboxetine versus the 100–127 ng/day read-across/CPCA value (Zhang et al. 2025; sponsor proposal, not a regulatory decision).

Industry refinement proposals, not adopted guidance: CPCA is a conservative de minimis screen that data should be allowed to refine (Ponting et al. 2024); a 150 ng/day floor for NDSRIs over 200 Da in Categories 1–2 (Bercu et al. 2024); best-practice read-across (Ponting et al. 2025).

Regional anchors: FDA 'Recommended Acceptable Intake Limits for NDSRIs' (final, August 2023; later revisions not verified); FDA 'Control of Nitrosamine Impurities in Human Drugs' (Revision 2 believed September 2024, unverified this session); EMA Q&A on the Article 5(3) referral on nitrosamine impurities (EMA/409815/2020, rolling revisions). ICH M7(R3) work aims to harmonise these.
commonDeficiencies: Relying on a negative standard Ames test to set 1.5 µg/day for a nitrosamine (not accepted without EAT and/or further data: Thomas et al. 2025; Zhang et al. 2025).
Read-across to a poorly matched surrogate; best-practice criteria are proposed by Ponting et al. 2025.
Using EMA Category 1 (18 ng/day) and FDA Category 1 (26.5 ng/day) interchangeably in a multi-region dossier (difference documented in Zhang et al. 2025).

notes.topic: What nitrosamine risk assessment and control should be built into a clinical-stage small-molecule drug substance?
notes.summary: Nitrosamines form when secondary, tertiary or quaternary amines, including the API itself, its amine-bearing impurities or degradants, amine reagents or solvent degradants, meet nitrosating agents. Sources include nitrite in reagents, water or excipients, sodium nitrite used to quench azide, recovered solvents, and NOx. APIs with a vulnerable amine can form NDSRIs, which compendial tests do not detect. An FDA simulation identified 446 secondary-amine-related impurities linked to 218 APIs and showed that API-fragment NDSRIs can exceed AIs under plausible conversion ratios. Control of amine-related impurities is therefore part of nitrosamine control. For clinical trials, industry data indicate the ICH M7 less-than-lifetime framework is protective for N-nitrosamines over typical trial durations. However, experts consulted in the EU Article 5(3) review questioned LTL for potent nitrosamines, so agency acceptance of LTL limits for cohort-of-concern impurities in trials should be confirmed rather than assumed. Formal agency expectations specific to IND/IMPD-stage nitrosamine assessments could not be confirmed this session.
keyPoints: Map every nitrosating-agent source and every amine (API, intermediates, reagents, solvents such as DMF/NMP degradants, quench steps) across the synthetic route; document in the impurity discussion (3.2.S.3.2).

Assess the API structure itself for NDSRI potential (secondary amine or nitrosatable tertiary amine). If vulnerable, consider CPCA category early, because it drives analytical sensitivity requirements.

Convert the AI to a specification-relevant concentration: limit (ppm) = AI (ng/day) ÷ maximum daily dose (mg/day). For example, 26.5 ng/day at 100 mg/day gives 0.265 ppm. The method LOQ must sit sufficiently below this value.
Use sensitive, specific LC-MS/MS or GC-MS methods. FDA researchers have published a Q14/Q2(R2)-enhanced-approach NDSRI method as a worked example (Zhang J et al. 2024).

Mitigations reported in the literature include avoiding nitrite/azide-quench chemistry near amines, controlling amine-related impurities, nitrite-scavenging antioxidants (for example ascorbic acid) in the drug product, and process redesign (Charoo et al. 2023; Holzgrabe 2023).

Nitrosamine findings in comparator or probe drugs can derail clinical studies: regulators stopped accepting rifampin in healthy-volunteer DDI studies after 1-methyl-4-nitrosopiperazine contamination (Paglialunga & van Haarst 2023).
commonDeficiencies: Risk assessment limited to small-molecule nitrosamines (NDMA/NDEA) without considering API-derived NDSRIs (Holzgrabe 2023; Yu et al. 2026).
Analytical LOQ not low enough relative to the AI-derived limit (practice-derived; see Zhang J et al. 2024 for method expectations).
Assuming LTL adjustment is automatically acceptable for N-nitrosamines (contested: Bercu et al. 2021 vs Article 5(3) expert view summarised by Wichitnithad et al. 2023).

notes.topic: How are residual solvent limits set for a drug substance (ICH Q3C classes, Option 1 vs Option 2, solvents without a PDE)?
notes.summary: ICH Q3C (original 1997) classifies solvents by risk and is maintained through PDE revisions. FDA announced revised PDEs for N-methylpyrrolidone and tetrahydrofuran (68 FR 64352, 13 Nov 2003) and for cumene (77 FR 10754, 23 Feb 2012), and a 2024 review lists Q3C(R9) as current. Class 1 solvents should be avoided: benzene, carbon tetrachloride, 1,2-dichloroethane, 1,1-dichloroethene and 1,1,1-trichloroethane, whose PDEs are unchanged since 1997. Class 2 solvents are limited by PDE, and Class 3 solvents have low toxic potential. Option 1 concentration limits (ppm) assume a 10 g/day dose. Option 2 calculates the limit from the PDE and the actual maximum daily dose. Solvents without an adequate PDE need a sponsor-derived PDE using Q3C's NOEL/safety-factor method. Like Q3A, Q3C is framed for marketing applications; the literature describes it as applicable from late development.
keyPoints: Test, in the drug substance specification, solvents used in or after the final synthetic steps, or justify their absence with purge data. Earlier-step solvents can be justified by process capability.
Option 1 ppm = PDE (mg/day) × 1000 ÷ 10 g/day. Option 2 ppm = PDE × 1000 ÷ actual dose (g/day), which allows higher limits for low-dose drugs.

Class 1 solvents: avoid unless strongly justified. A 2025 review argues the Class 1 PDEs (except benzene) merit revision, that two could be handled as M7 mutagenic carcinogens, and challenges the 10 g/day assumption (Snodin 2025; proposal, not guideline).

Example sponsor-derived PDEs: diisopropyl ether 0.98 mg/day, about 98 ppm at 10 g/day (Romanelli & Evandri 2018); 2-methyltetrahydrofuran 50 mg/day from a 3-month GLP rat study, NOAEL 250 mg/kg/day (Parris et al. 2017). Whether a given solvent has since been added to Q3C with an official PDE should be checked against the current Q3C revision.
Solvent changes between toxicology and clinical batches, or a new solvent, should be flagged in 3.2.S.2.6 and reassessed.
commonDeficiencies: Use of a solvent with no Q3C PDE and no derived, documented PDE (illustrated by DIPE and 2-MeTHF literature that had to derive PDEs).
Applying Option 1 concentration limits to a solvent whose PDE-based limit at the actual dose would differ, without stating which option is used (practice-derived).

notes.topic: How should elemental impurities, such as residual metal catalysts, be addressed for a drug substance in clinical development and at marketing?
notes.summary: ICH Q3D sets permitted daily exposures (PDEs) for elemental impurities by route and requires a risk assessment of the drug product. That assessment covers contributions from the drug substance (notably intentionally added catalysts such as Pd, Pt, Ni, Ru, Rh), excipients, water, manufacturing equipment and container closure. Elements are controlled when the assessment indicates levels could exceed the control threshold of 30% of the PDE. Assessment may use a component approach (Option 2b, built from supplier and component data) or finished-product testing (Option 3). A published comparison found component estimates conservative relative to measured ICP-MS results. Option 1 concentration limits (assuming 10 g/day) give, for example, 0.5 µg/g for oral lead and cadmium. As recalled by the author, Q3D excludes products used during clinical research stages, but its PDEs are the usual benchmark for clinical-stage catalyst limits.
keyPoints: Drug substance: for each intentionally added metal catalyst or reagent, either specify a limit in the drug substance (3.2.S.4.1) or justify purge with batch data; base the limit on the PDE for the intended route and the dose.

Drug product risk assessment: summarise potential sources, expected levels versus 30% of PDE, and the resulting control; Option 2b (component) and Option 3 (product) approaches are both used (Hamidallah et al. 2025; 24 elements by ICP-MS per USP <233> in that study).
Shared excipient elemental-impurity databases can reduce excipient testing in the risk assessment (Torres et al. 2021).
Option 1 example concentrations: Pb and Cd 0.5 µg/g (oral), consistent with PDEs of 5 µg/day at 10 g/day (Jurowski & Krośniak 2022).

Revisions: Q3D(R1) and Q3D(R2) (R2 believed April 2022, adding cutaneous/transcutaneous PDEs and correcting some PDEs) are listed as current in a 2024 review; exact dates were not verified this session.
commonDeficiencies: Catalyst limits set from analytical capability rather than the route-specific PDE and dose (practice-derived).
Drug product risk assessment omits the drug substance contribution from catalysts (practice-derived).

notes.topic: How are regulatory starting materials selected and justified for a synthetic drug substance (ICH Q11), and when must this be settled?
notes.summary: ICH Q11 (ICH Step 4 2012; FDA notice of availability 77 FR 69634, 20 Nov 2012) harmonises how drug-substance development and manufacturing process information is presented in CTD sections. It applies to chemical and biotechnological/biological entities, and its Section 5 sets general principles for selecting starting materials. Changes early in a synthesis have lower potential to affect drug-substance quality. Enough of the process must be described in the application for regulators to understand how impurities form, carry over and are purged, so steps that affect the impurity profile should normally fall within the application. A starting material should be a substance of defined chemical properties and structure, normally isolated rather than a non-isolated intermediate, and incorporated as a significant structural fragment. GMP applies from the point the starting material is introduced. A later ICH Q11 Q&A on selection and justification of starting materials (believed August 2017) clarified that the principles are applied together, not one at a time, and addressed commercially available chemicals. Industry authors argue for science- and risk-based selection.
keyPoints: Marketing (3.2.S.2.3): propose each starting material with a justification against the Q11 principles and a specification (identity, assay/purity, impurities able to carry through), supported by impurity fate and purge data.
Convergent syntheses: each branch begins with a starting material; apply the principles to every branch.
Commercially available chemicals sold as commodities in non-pharmaceutical markets can be designated with lighter justification (Q11/Q11 Q&A concept; check the exact wording in the Q&A).

Phase 1 IND/IMPD: describe the route from purchased materials with a flow chart; formal starting-material agreement is normally sought before pivotal/registration batches (for example at end-of-phase-2 in the US). The timing comes from FDA's 2003 phase 2/3 CMC guidance as recalled and was not re-verified.
EU: an EMA reflection paper on the selection and justification of starting materials (believed EMA/448443/2014) preceded the Q11 Q&A; confirm its current status.
Redefining starting materials late (for example moving to a more advanced intermediate) is a common source of major questions at MAA/NDA; plan the designation early.
commonDeficiencies: Proposing an advanced intermediate as a starting material so that steps affecting the impurity profile fall outside the dossier (the concern that motivated the Q11 Q&A; Watson et al. 2016 discuss the debate).
Starting material specifications without impurity limits linked to fate/purge data (practice-derived).

notes.topic: How much drug-substance manufacturing and control information (3.2.S.2) is needed for a first-in-human IND or IMPD compared with later phases and marketing?
notes.summary: Under 21 CFR 312.23(a)(7), CMC information in an IND should ensure the identification, quality, purity and strength of the investigational drug, and its amount depends on the phase, duration and dosage form. For the drug substance, sponsors provide a description including physical, chemical or biological characteristics, the manufacturer's name and address, the general method of preparation, acceptable limits and analytical methods, and information supporting stability. FDA's 1995 Phase 1 guidance, as recalled, expects a brief process description with a flow chart and the reagents, solvents and catalysts used. It does not expect detailed process controls or validation at phase 1. It directs sponsors to signals of potential risk such as impure components, structures of known toxicity, instability, or an impurity profile that indicates a hazard or is too poorly defined to assess. Detail increases through phase 2/3 (FDA 2003 phase 2/3 CMC guidance). At marketing, ICH Q11 expects a full process description with critical process parameters, controls of critical steps, justified starting materials and process development history. In an FY2013 CDER review of initial INDs, CMC was the most frequent reason for clinical hold. In EU CTA deficiency letters, incomplete descriptions of manufacturing controls and critical process parameters recur.
keyPoints: FIH minimum: manufacturer(s) and sites; synthetic scheme/flow chart from purchased materials with reagents, solvents and catalysts; batch formula or scale for the clinical batch; in-process controls where they ensure safety; a list of batches used in toxicology and clinical studies with their route/process version.
Explain differences between the toxicology batch and the clinical batch (route, scale, site, impurity profile) in 3.2.S.2.6, because impurity qualification depends on comparability.
US phase 1 information is scaled to risk (21 CFR 312.23(a)(7)(i)); the reviewer's question is whether the material is safe for the proposed trial.
Phase 2/3: add process detail, reprocessing, critical steps and controls, and begin starting-material justification (FDA 2003 phase 2/3 guidance; recalled, not re-verified).

Marketing: ICH Q11 content in 3.2.S.2.2–3.2.S.2.6 (process description with CPPs, materials with SM justification, controls of critical steps and intermediates, process development), plus process validation/evaluation as regionally required.
EU: EMA/CHMP/QWP/834816/2015 defines IMPD content by section and phase; exact phase-specific wording was not verified this session.
commonDeficiencies: CMC was the most commonly cited reason for clinical hold among 125 of 1410 initial CDER INDs (8.9%) placed on hold in FY2013 (Lapteva & Pariser 2016).
Incomplete descriptions of manufacturing controls and critical process parameters in IMPDs (Arsić et al. 2026).
No explanation of process differences between toxicology and clinical batches (practice-derived).

notes.topic: What solid-form (polymorph, solvate, amorphous, salt or cocrystal) information and controls are expected for a drug substance at each development stage?
notes.summary: Solid form is a drug-substance critical quality attribute whenever forms differ in solubility, dissolution, stability or processability. ICH Q6A Decision Tree #4 asks three questions in turn. Can different polymorphs form (screening)? Do they differ in relevant properties? Does drug product performance depend on form? Where it does, acceptance criteria for polymorphic content are set in the drug substance and monitored in the drug product if needed. The ritonavir case is the reference failure: a more stable, previously unknown Form II appeared in 1998, slowed dissolution, compromised oral bioavailability and forced withdrawal of the capsule formulation. FDA reviewers' analysis for generics (2004) produced decision trees for when polymorphs must be monitored and concluded that polymorphism is not relevant to drug-substance 'sameness'. Cocrystals have specific FDA guidance and an EMA reflection paper.
keyPoints: FIH: identify and characterise the solid form of the toxicology and clinical batches (for example XRPD, DSC/TGA, water sorption, microscopy) and state it in 3.2.S.1.3/3.2.S.3.1; confirm the same form across batches used in nonclinical and clinical studies.
Complete a polymorph/solvate screen and select the commercial form before pivotal clinical and stability batches. A late form change can require bridging (bioavailability and stability) studies.
Use Q6A Decision Tree #4 logic to decide whether a polymorph test belongs in the drug substance specification (3.2.S.4.1) and whether form must be monitored in the drug product.

High-energy forms (metastable polymorphs, amorphous) need a transformation-risk assessment covering manufacturing stresses and storage, analytical detection limits for the undesired form, and biopharmaceutical impact; Kestur et al. (2022) give workflows and case studies.
Process development must control which form crystallises (seeding, solvent, supersaturation) and show the form is stable on storage (3.2.S.7) (Lee, Erdemir & Myerson 2011).

Cocrystals: FDA has issued guidance on regulatory classification of pharmaceutical cocrystals (original and revision dates not verified this session) and EMA a reflection paper on cocrystals (Thipparaboina et al. 2016 note both).
commonDeficiencies: No solid-form characterisation of clinical batches, or a form different from the toxicology batch without assessment (practice-derived).
Undetected conversion to a more stable, less soluble form: the ritonavir precedent (Morissette et al. 2003).

notes.topic: What stability data support a drug-substance retest period for phase 1, and how can it be extended or predicted?
notes.summary: ICH Q1A(R2) (FDA notice 68 FR 65717, 21 Nov 2003) and Q1E (FDA notice 69 FR 32010, 8 June 2004) govern the stability data and evaluation used to propose a registration retest period. For phase 1, US requirements are lighter. As recalled from FDA's 1995 Phase 1 guidance, the sponsor briefly describes the stability study and test methods used to show the drug substance is stable for the duration of the toxicology and clinical studies, rather than submitting full data or protocols. EU IMPDs state a retest period from available data, and the IMPD guideline is understood to allow later extension under a pre-stated protocol (wording not verified). Accelerated Stability Assessment Program (ASAP) studies combine a humidity-corrected Arrhenius model with isoconversion to give predictive retest estimates in weeks. In an AstraZeneca comparison across 10 drug substances, ASAP predictions were conservative relative to ICH-compliant data. Where an ASAP study showed minimal degradation, it supported an initial retest period of at least 12 months.
keyPoints: FIH package (3.2.S.7): stress/forced-degradation results showing the assay/impurity method is stability-indicating; available real-time and accelerated data on a representative batch; the proposed retest period and storage condition; and a commitment or protocol for continued testing.

ASAP: run short-term high-temperature/humidity studies designed to drive the shelf-life-limiting degradant to its specification level, then fit the moisture-modified Arrhenius model (Waterman 2011). Predictions have been verified against long-term data, including 12-month real-time data for an early-phase capsule (Modhave et al. 2024).

Retest-period extensions during the trial should be data-driven (ongoing real-time data on the same or representative batch) and follow the stated protocol; document them in IND amendments/annual reports (US) or as allowed by the IMPD protocol (EU).

Registration: Q1A(R2) long-term, intermediate and accelerated conditions on primary batches, evaluated per Q1E (extrapolation limits, statistical analysis). Exact batch-number and duration requirements should be checked against the guideline text.

Revision watch: a consolidated ICH Q1 (merging Q1A–Q1F and Q5C) was released as a Step 2 draft in 2025 (as recalled). Its status as of 2026-10 was not established, and whether it adds explicit clinical-phase provisions was not verified.
commonDeficiencies: Missing or insufficient stability data in the IMPD, one of the most frequently cited CTA deficiencies (Arsić et al. 2026).
Retest period claimed without showing the method is stability-indicating (practice-derived).

notes.topic: What GMP standard applies to drug substance and investigational product manufactured for phase 1 trials?
notes.summary: FDA's final rule of 15 July 2008 (73 FR 40453) amended the CGMP regulations to exempt most phase 1 investigational drugs from 21 CFR part 211. FDA continues oversight under its statutory CGMP authority and through IND review, and issued a companion guidance, 'CGMP for Phase 1 Investigational Drugs' (dated November 2007). An earlier direct final rule of 17 January 2006 (71 FR 2458) pursued the same exemption with a draft guidance. The exemption does not extend to material once it is used in phase 2/3 or to lawfully marketed drugs, per 21 CFR 210.2(c) as recalled. For the API itself, ICH Q7 (2000) Section 19 describes GMP appropriate to APIs for use in clinical trials. Controls rise with development stage, and full Q7 applies to commercial API from the introduction of the starting material. In the EU, IMP manufacture follows the GMP rules for investigational medicinal products under the Clinical Trials Regulation framework; the specific instrument and date were not verified this session.
keyPoints: US phase 1: CGMP is still required by statute, with part 211 detail replaced by the phase 1 guidance approach (written procedures, controlled facilities and equipment, quality control function, records, testing and release appropriate to phase 1).
The phase 1 exemption ends when the same material is used in phase 2/3 (210.2(c), as recalled). Plan GMP upgrades of drug-substance supply before phase 2.
API for clinical trials: apply ICH Q7 Section 19 principles (controls appropriate to stage, documentation of process changes, release by an independent quality unit).
Record and disclose in the IND/IMPD the manufacturer and site of each drug-substance batch and the process version used, so batch histories link to toxicology qualification.
commonDeficiencies: Treating the phase 1 exemption as exempting material later reused in phase 2 (practice-derived; based on the rule's scope).

notes.topic: Which drug-substance CMC deficiencies most often delay first-in-human INDs and CTAs, and how are they pre-empted?
notes.summary: FDA CDER received 1410 initial INDs in fiscal year 2013. Of these, 125 (8.9%) were placed on clinical hold within the 30-day review, and CMC was the most commonly cited reason, ahead of clinical and toxicology. More than half of the held INDs became active within a year. Hold rates and reasons did not differ between rare- and common-disease or commercial and research INDs, and the authors concluded many holds could be avoided by following available guidance. A retrospective analysis of 74 deficiency letters for 26 EU clinical trial applications (2015–2024) found the most prominent IMPD deficiencies were inadequately justified or incomplete specifications, missing or insufficient stability data, and incomplete descriptions of manufacturing controls and critical process parameters. These occurred across chemical, biological and ATMP products. In mutagenic-impurity sections, FDA reviewers escalate (Q)SAR packages that use a single methodology, conflict with model output without explanation, or rely on outdated software.
keyPoints: Specifications: every acceptance criterion should trace to batch data and to toxicology-batch qualification, and the analytical methods should be shown fit for purpose (3.2.S.4).
Stability: include stress data, available real-time/accelerated data and a clear retest period with an extension plan (3.2.S.7).
Process: give a flow chart, materials, critical steps and controls appropriate to phase, and differences between toxicology and clinical batches (3.2.S.2).

Impurities: provide an M7 assessment with two complementary (Q)SAR methods and documented expert review, a nitrosamine risk assessment, and residual solvent and elemental impurity considerations (3.2.S.3.2).
Use pre-IND or scientific-advice meetings for non-standard approaches, such as duration-adjusted impurity limits or Option 4 purge arguments.
commonDeficiencies: CMC issues are the leading cause of initial-IND clinical holds (FY2013 CDER data; Lapteva & Pariser 2016).
Inadequately justified or incomplete specifications; missing or insufficient stability data; incomplete manufacturing control and CPP descriptions (Arsić et al. 2026).
(Q)SAR submissions using one methodology, poorly documented, or with unexplained conclusions (Amberg et al. 2019).
